I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better?
  • According to recent reports, you'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up.
  • In a recent development, proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

According to recent reports, you'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

In a recent development, proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it.".

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

Recent findings suggest that what's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

Sources indicate that however, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

It has been revealed that image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

According to recent reports, I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran highlighted that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Sources indicate that increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minor spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

According to recent reports, the Hunger Games movies (which are streaming with a Hulu subscription) have entertained audiences for over ten years, and we've got yet another book to screen adaptation in theaters now thanks to Francis Lawrence's Sunrise on the Reaping film. My favorite scene from the book was unfortunately cut from the prequel movie, and I had to ask both the director and actress Mckenna Grace about it.

I loved the Sunrise on the Reaping book, and was wildly impressed by how well it was adapted for film. Unfortunately, the scene where Maysilee kills a Gamemaker alongside District 4 career Maritte didn't make it. As you can see in the video above, I asked Francis Lawrence about this decision, where he confirmed the sequence was shot during principal photography. In his words:.

It's probably the most debated sequence that we had throughout the development process. What happens is, because of that action with the game makers and because of the fight that happens with Maysilee and Haymitch after, it was a fight that in the book is about implicit submission. And the argument that some of us had was that he was already no longer submitting. Like, you know, if you've been down to Sub A, if you've done the things that he's done without spoiler in this movie he's not submitting anymore. And so it didn't feel like it thematically fit.

Industry observers note that points were made. While it would have been awesome to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker, in the novel it's connected to her relationship with Haymitch. They have an argument afterward about him still implicitly submitting to The Capitol, and not killing the Gamemakers despite being the closest Tribute to them. As director Francis Lawrence told me, that confrontation between the District 12 tributes didn't make sense for the movie adaptation, especially after following Joseph Zada's protagonist as he attempted to break The Arena.

According to recent reports, this sequence was indeed shot, so the debate about whether or not to include it in Sunrise on the Reaping extended to the post-production phase. As the director went on to tell me:.

We shot it. We even augmented the fight to be, tried to be about different things. And then that thematically didn't fit. And so we ended up cutting it from the movie, but I believe will be one of the deleted scenes that will be available.

Fingers crossed that we get to see this scene sometime in the future, via special features when the latest Hunger Games prequel is released to homes. This isn't the only change made to Sunrise on the Reaping, which included some references to Lucy Gray Baird from Songbirds and Snakes. Of course, I had to ask the actress who brought Maysilee to life about the cut sequence.

While interviewing the cast of the new Hunger Games movie, I asked Mckenna Grace about Maysilee's cut scene. She spoke about the argument with Joseph Zada's Haymitch that followed the Gamemaker death, telling me:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that that argument scene was one of my favorite things that I got to do because it was just Joe and I in the woods like screaming at each other. I think that what it was, was it didn't make sense for our characters to be split at that time because we didn't have enough time to repair it like they did in the book. And we didn't have the scene, you know, where they're splitting the sardines like in the book. And so it just didn't make, it didn't make sense for them to be so split at that time whenever their bond had just become so strong. Because they didn't get to reforge it and go and burn through the hedge together.

In a recent development, points were made. As awesome as it would have been to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker with one of her poisoned darts, that sequence also complicated her relationship with Haymitch shortly before her death. Instead, Francis Lawrence and organization decided to keep the District 12 tributes as a united force until Mckenna Grace's character was killed by bird mutts. As such, the death and Haymitch's reaction are given extra emotional weight.

According to recent reports, adapting novels for film is a tough task, and there's always some content that ends up on the cutting room floor. Francis Lawrence has directed almost all of the Hunger Games movies, so he knows all too well what this process is like. While Sunrise on the Reaping's reviews were mixed, I think that it was a wildly successful film version of the devastating novel.

According to recent reports, the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. Panem is once again on the substantial screen, here's to hoping that we get another prequel from author Suzanne Collins soon.

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

Sources indicate that this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

Hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

While Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

According to recent reports, with 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

And on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

Okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. So initially, you were called the Joe Rogan of the left. Recently, you’ve stated you operate more like a Charlie Kirk. Is that the right analog for the kind of influence you want to have? And if not, is there another?

In a recent development, I don’t think there is an appropriate analog because I’m everything all at once at the same time, because I work out and I do collaborations with people who are not expressly political, so that’s kind of like Joe Rogan. I go out and operate sometimes as a campaign surrogate, and I do rallies at college campuses and I deliver speeches, so that’s kind of like Charlie Kirk. But then usually my day-to-day commentary is what I like to jokingly refer to as a Rush Limbaugh for Zoomers. So I do all of those things at the same time, and that’s, I think, part of the reason why it’s so hard to make sense of what I do from the perspective of someone who just doesn’t understand Twitch or doesn’t understand exactly what I’m doing and has only seen negatively framed clips or clips out of context, that kind of thing. Having stated that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

Okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. And I think about [Zohran] Mamdani in this case. I just—.

It has been revealed that maybe because of that Rush Limbaugh–esque heightened rhetoric; do you agree with that characterization? And how does that make you feel?

Well, my feelings are immaterial in this. As long as they’re delivering, I think that’s what matters. I’ve mentioned this before: I love Zohran and, off the rip, my attitude on this was always just put the policies in the bag. If you’re delivering for the people of New York, and if you’re delivering successfully and every success that you have as a democratic socialist mayor of New York bodes well for the rest of this movement, then I’m happy.

In a recent development, yeah, but are you talking to him behind the scenes? There’s still a relationship there? Because honestly—.

Yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too newly introduced for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a major part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So on that front, of course they got to do what they got to do.

So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

Recent findings suggest that I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

So we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

As far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

Sources indicate that I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Industry observers note that can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Industry observers note that yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

Recent findings suggest that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Recent findings suggest that yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

No, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

Recent findings suggest that and I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

Recent findings suggest that you’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically noted, “Look, everybody claims silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of issues that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

According to recent reports, I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

It has been revealed that okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve said some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

And I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Quote: “If you cared about Medicare fraud, you’d kill Rick Scott.” You’ve mentioned things that you wish you had said differently. Do you regret anything that you’ve said? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

Yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve mentioned and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

Okay. But you also said that you are a role model.

Can you parse that a little bit?

Yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate. The rude behavior that I demonstrate is what people get frustrated by or what they attack, but—.

Sources indicate that yeah, I am vulgar, for sure. But I think the systems of violence and oppression that people are subjected to [are] far worse than any vulgar thing I could have ever remarked. And we kind of saw this dynamic play itself out on the campaign trail as well. And I think the finality of it all came with Haley Stevens, when she decided to lean into the “Hasan Piker is such a problem that I'm leaving the Democratic Party and endorsing the Republican platform.” [That] was, I think in some respects, a wake-up call because it forced everyone to go, Wait a minute. No, those guys are actually far worse. What are we talking about? Right? Because at the end of the day, Donald Trump is not only vulgar, but he’s also violent. And sure, I’m vulgar, but ultimately I’m fighting for social justice. I’m fighting for people who are dispossessed, people who don’t get heard at all. I’m trying to offer them a voice, a platform for their frustrations, and communicate their desires, their anxieties.

Do you think the vulgarity actually helps you with your audience? Because if they’re young men, men in their 20s, it’s like the edgelord vernacular.

In a recent development, certainly, but I don’t do it for some tactical purpose. I do it because that’s just who I am.

I mean, I always say, look, if you go after marginalized people, vulnerable populations, and you bully them, I’m gonna bully you. Someone has to do it.

For what it’s worth, you’re being very civil right now.

Oh yeah. I mean, this is a very different format. I am very different in these sorts of professional settings than I am on my own broadcast where I’m offering off-the-cuff commentary on these hot-button issues.

Is this more performative, or is that?

I would say this is more performative.

I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

But what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

Industry observers note that yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

No. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

The comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

But that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

Recent findings suggest that I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this problem in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s important to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you noted and the way your audience responded?

According to recent reports, no, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I said something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

So speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve said you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

In a recent development, so what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

According to recent reports, I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

So here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The problem, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

Industry observers note that I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

According to recent reports, and also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

According to recent reports, but there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

According to recent reports, immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. I think that, by and large, they have a profoundly key task that they have to accomplish. Their presence is supposed to invoke law and order. Their presence sometimes invokes lawlessness and disorder. That’s unacceptable. They’re very well paid. They have the best unions. Do your jobs better. That’s my attitude on policing. So it’s antagonistic, but it’s also a demand that I’m making from this institution that I truly do believe is important for society to function. That’s one way to tackle this issue in a way that Americans understand. I like to call it chudifying your commentary. Zohran does a very good job of libifying his commentary. He’s very liberal-appealing. I like to do the opposite. I like to chudify it. I appeal to the chuds. I speak from that tone and that language when I advocate for certain things.

In a recent development, yeah, edgelord vernacular, sure. But it’s kind of like, whether we’re talking about abortions or whether we’re talking about transgender bills, like anti-trans bills, I’m like, I don’t want the fucking government getting involved in these affairs. What do you want? You want some creepy pervert to do penis inspection day at your high school? What are you, a pervert? Are you a pedophile? I want small government when it comes to this kind of stuff. And that is a way to argue from a perspective that I think right-wingers can understand.

According to recent reports, switching gears, we talked a little bit about suits for a second, but I want to talk about style more largely. So at the RNC’s midterm convention in September, there was a 25-foot selfie of you in underwear displayed on the jumbotron. How do you think about that?

It’s a strange thing because I wish I was as in shape right now as I was, because that was peak.

Thank you. But also at the same time, I’m like, Oh, I wish I looked like that right now.

Industry observers note that why do you think they’re so obsessed with your looks? What is going on there? How is that helpful to them actually?

It’s not. I think about that quite a bit. I think…they’re gay.

That’s it. I think they’re in the closet. There are a lot of Republican operatives that are just either gay or in the closet and haven’t been able to figure out how to communicate their desires. So they were just frustrated and confused. But there’s no other reason to have this pathological, this psychosexual, obsession where you’re like, “My opponent, this political opponent, is a dangerous guy. He’s a radical communist, Islamist, jihadist.”.

Industry observers note that “And he’s also sexy. Look at him shirtless. Look at him shirtless.” Because I thought these guys were peak masculinity. I thought that’s what they were about. The Joe Rogan Experience, you know, Brazilian jiujitsu, and working out was supposed to be the thing in the right.

There’s nothing unmasculine about being gay.

Recent findings suggest that I’m kidding. That’s not how they think of it. I know.

And not only that, but also, ultimately, why are they showing a shirtless photo of me where I look jacked?

Sources indicate that yeah. Okay. But it’s not just the GOP. Almost any coverage of you, including now this, includes a reference to your appearance. And I’m sorry we’re doing this right now.

Do you like it in some regard, or does it bother you?

It’s attention. I like it. In the past, when people would approach me and be like, “Why is The Upcoming York Times only talking about how you look and not talking about your ideas?” I was like, “Look, that is terrorism insurance.” If I’m getting into these legacy publishers and not being called a terrorist and instead being called a hot guy, I’ll take it.

Okay. Okay. One last question about your looks. If Calvin Klein calls tomorrow and wants you to do the Houston Street billboard, are you doing it?

Sources indicate that I would need to immediately get on a steroid regimen. I would need to look like Kumail Nanjiani before.

I mean, yeah, I would do it. Why wouldn’t I do it?

Okay. I wonder, with your audience, because there are a bunch of young guys looking up to a guy who’s maybe slightly older than them, looks like they might want to look, is that homoerotic at all?

It has been revealed that but I do have a fairly queer community as well. We do a census. We do a yearly census. Fourteen percent of my audience is trans, which is obviously much higher than the American population.

What are some other demos that would be interesting that we wouldn’t expect?

Well, the classic ones are obviously—it’s like 60% white men under the age of 35.

You perform best with all the people that Vanity Fair performs worst [with].

It has been revealed that I think a lot of mainstream outlets are really bad at captivating the attention of young men in particular. That’s probably part of the reason why people are always fascinated with this group. They’re trying to understand it.

What about you captured them? How did you do it?

According to recent reports, I was a young man at some point, and I also have the same interests, and I think that’s part of it. And I also speak—going back to the crude, the language that I deploy, the vulgar language that I deploy, it’s like I speak like a normal person. I speak and get angry in the same exact ways that normal people do.

Industry observers note that all right. Hasan, what’s your attitude toward money? How do you think about money?

It has been revealed that for me personally, it has a corrosive influence, I think. It has the capacity to make you unbelievably out of touch. It’s something that I think about quite a bit in my own personal experience. I was a very stubborn person with air travel. Even when I had a little bit of additional income, I refused to pay the extra for the economy-plus seats.

It has been revealed that I’m a major dude. I’m 6’4”, I can’t fit in the seats, and I would still. It’s a point of pride. Until one day I was put in a business class seat for some kind of business travel. And at that point I had enough money to purchase business class seats on my own, and I was like, I’m never looking back.

In a recent development, you were ruined. You were ruined.

Recent findings suggest that it ruined me. It completely ruined me. So now—.

Tina Brown notes that the private plane ruins people, that when you see how that works, it’s over. Hook, line, sinker, people are done.

That corruption is almost—she doesn't say this, but I’m interpreting that it’s almost inevitable after that.

Yes. I think that every instance of financial stability or financial freedom that I’ve gained has made me more out of step with the struggles that I used to experience and the struggle that everyday people experience. And I think you have to always be in touch. Especially in my line of work, you have to understand where people are. On the other hand, though, it is editorial freedom, because I have been able to maintain complete editorial control, complete editorial freedom, because I am completely unbought, completely unbossed, completely unshackled. There have been numerous instances where I’ve obviously had contracts with Amazon and stuff like that because I know I need to play ball also to make sure that I am a reliable team player so they don’t deplatform me. However, there have been so many instances where people have come to me with tremendous sponsorship opportunities.

Polymarket is one that I talk about all the time. [For] 2024 election night, their opening salvo was a million dollars just to have their ticker on the side. I said, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling company, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.

So Calvin Klein would be an exception.

Calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.

Some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?

Great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?

Because you stated you differentiate with net worth.

I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—.

Sources indicate that the capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.

It has been revealed that all right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?

How To Solve All Main Puzzles In GTA 6′s Tenebrae Lux

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Kotaku

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you decide you’d rather sit at home all day and play a pretentious, cerebral puzzle game instead of go on heists, Tenebrae Lux is waiting for Jason and Lucia on their JoyStation in GTA VI.
  • According to recent reports, but I’m assuming you’re here because you either want to beat it rapidly, or you’ve gotten so stuck (as I did) on a few of the puzzles that you’re desperate for help.
  • You can’t do much: just walk around and examine objects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6Grand Theft Auto VI.

If you decide you’d rather sit at home all day and play a pretentious, cerebral puzzle game instead of go on heists, Tenebrae Lux is waiting for Jason and Lucia on their JoyStation in GTA VI. While on the surface it looks like just a funny gag poking at auteur culture (and one developer in particular), Tenebrae Lux is a surprisingly solid, short puzzle game that (if you’re not using this guide) may take you a few hours to get through.

According to recent reports, but I’m assuming you’re here because you either want to beat it rapidly, or you’ve gotten so stuck (as I did) on a few of the puzzles that you’re desperate for help. I get you. Here’s as simple a walkthrough as I could manage for Tenebrae Lux:.

You’ll start out on the shoreline. You can’t do much: just walk around and examine objects. To start with, you’re going to want to head to the left side of the shore (assuming you’re facing the shore from the beach you start on) where there are multiple run-down shacks lit by massive bright lights.

Inside these shacks are three puzzles on gridded boards. On those grids, multiple pieces are placed with different 3D shapes atop: three-tiered tall ones, middling spiky ones, and flat ones with a tiny dot in the middle. The flat ones don’t move at all, the middle-sized spiky ones can slide across the board and clear the flat ones if they land next to them, and the three-tiered tall ones and middle-sized ones clear one another in the same fashion. Your goal is to clear all the pieces off the board.

Industry observers note that you can do these puzzles in any order. One of them is easy and straightforward, but the other two require a little bit more thinking. You’ll have to use the fact that the flat pieces don’t move and cannot be cleared by the three-tiered pieces to set up the three-tiers so they and the mountain pieces can clear one another once all the flat ones are off the board.

Sources indicate that the three main puzzles in this area should be fairly simple to do, though there are a couple of hidden ones you can optionally do that are more difficult. On at least one, you might need to set up your board so you have two three-tier pieces set up with a gap between them that a middle-sized piece can easily get into after clearing a flat one. See below:.

When I move that mountain-shaped piece to the left, it will take out itself and all three of those other tiles with it.

This puzzle will easily make you feel like you’re losing your mind, but I highly recommend trying to work it out for yourself first, if you can.

When you enter the room upstairs in the bunker, you enter a loop that will keep perpetuating each time you go through the door and up the stairs. The room will be almost identical each time you enter it, but for two things. The first will be the calendar, which will show the date as being one of six different dates, and the second will be one of the other objects in the room.

Your goal is to find a six-digit code and enter it into the phone, followed by the # sign, to proceed.

In order to get the code, you need to pay attention to what day it is, and what is different in the room on that date. If you keep going up the stairs over and over, the dates will eventually cycle back through, so if you miss one don’t worry, you can keep going to see it again. The dates are as follows: October 11, 14, 20, 23, 27, and 30. You won’t see the dates in any particular order, but you’ll need to put them in that order when you input the numbers for each date into the phone.

Industry observers note that the numbers themselves, you get from finding what’s “different” in the room on a given date, and working out what number the difference corresponds to. There are ten possible differences, and your playthrough won’t have all these objects in the room—it’s random each time, though consistent within a single playthrough of the puzzle. Here are the ten possible differences:.

Once you get the code right, exit upwards one last time and on you go.

This one was waaaaay more confusing to me than it needed to be. The goal is to cross the bridge off to the left of the ruins. The bridge has multiple rows of weird symbols on it. You have to walk over the correct symbol in order to proceed. If you walk over the wrong one, a lamp will go out. If you do it wrong three times, you fail and the puzzle resets.

The trick to figuring out the correct symbols is in the ruins and the poem on the plaque just outside.

The ruins will contain the following items, which correspond to the following descriptors in each of the seven lines of the poem:.

The items will be scattered across the ruins. Also in the ruins you will find a bunch of weird, esoteric symbols glowing on the ruined archways above. These symbols correspond to the symbols on the bridge.

To solve this, you need to visit each of the items in the order they appear in the poem, and match the item with the symbol on the ruins that corresponds to it, then follow the symbols across the bridge in order (the direction they’re facing doesn’t matter). It can be a bit tricky to figure out which symbol goes with which item. The best way I can describe it is the symbol for each item is the one that’s over the doorway “entrance” to each item, so the one you have to pass under to reach it.

In a recent development, here’s a map to show you what I mean. Orange circles are places where the objects can appear, and green triangles are where symbols are. I’ve numbered them, but please don’t mistake the numbers for the correct order of the objects: that’s going to be determined by the poem, and the poem’s order is random.

Also note that #1 below is on the ground, because the arch has collapsed.

This can still be confusing, so let me walk you through what I got as an example. Here’s my poem:.

First up is moon, which for me was straight ahead through the first door.

Two days of rest states nothing, so we move to the third line, which mentions forests. Here’s the tree:.

Recent findings suggest that third verse mentions gold, then earth, in order. My trophy was past the mark that had crumbled to the ground, and my earth was at the very start of the puzzle:.

This next line is a bit tricky, as it mentions both sun and moon. But there are only seven lines on the bridge, and the items are only used one time each. So we just focus on sun here. I didn’t get a good picture of my sundial, sorry!

The last two lines in order mentions fire first, then drinking, which is water. Here’s fire:.

So I’d follow those symbols in order across the bridge. It may help to draw a map on a piece of scrap paper or in a notebook for this one so you don’t have to slowly walk back and forth over and over.

If you fail, the puzzle will fully reset itself, and you’ll have to look at a new version of the poem and ruins and try again.

Industry observers note that this bit is a little creepy and again confusing at first, but quite easy once you work it out. All you have to do is walk in the door that’s the furthest away from any of the figures walking through the doors.

In the photo above, the man is walking toward the third door from the right, so I want to go to the farthest door on the left.

It has been revealed that as you go, more figures will start to appear. When there are multiple, you want to try and split the distance as best as possible. You also have to avoid any doors that say they’re out of order, so if they have a sign on them, go to the next one furthest away from the man. On the last set of doors, there was no way to get away from the men, so I just walked directly between two of them.

Once you pass through the last door, you’ve officially beaten Tenebrae Lux!

The best way to play is just to experience the game, even if most of us are too internet-pilled to do that.

People don't like having to scroll a significant number back and forth to deposit a specific amount.

Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change.
  • In a recent development, download your playlist as a .txt file.
  • In a recent development, install Python on your system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

In a recent development, download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

In a recent development, install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Industry observers note that download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Recent findings suggest that sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

According to recent reports, have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Recent findings suggest that like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of upcoming-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection.".

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. People can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

According to recent reports, if you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Pick your speaker on your wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Industry observers note that plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Industry observers note that tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:.

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

According to recent reports, force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

Set your levels with the mixer’s faders.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:.

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

Recent findings suggest that my cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

According to recent reports, it's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:.

It has been revealed that your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Sources indicate that most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:.

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

Sources indicate that this isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is one of the most comfortable pillows I’ve tested for Tom's Guide, and more than lives up to its luxury $135 price tag. A shredded memory foam and latex fill hugs your head while supporting your neck no matter the position you sleep in. The shredded foam and cotton cover also keeps the pillow breathable and cool even on warm nights. However, while the Saatva Cloud delivered supreme comfort, heavy and tall side sleepers who need firmer support should look elsewhere.

Comfy for all sleeping positions.

Lacks firm support for tall and heavy bodies.

Saatva is the luxury sleep brand behind the number one rated option in our best mattress of the year guide, the Saatva Classic (see our Saatva Classic mattress review), which is why I'm always eager to test the Saatva's sleep accessories that deliver the brand's signature luxury for less. Along with its mattress toppers and bed sheets, Saatva also offers a line-up of premium pillows, one of which is the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

Filled with shredded gel-infused memory foam, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow promises universal support and comfort — so I tested it for a week to see if it's worthy of a place in our best pillow guide.

Despite the name, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow isn't made completely out of memory foam; it also contains natural latex. And after testing it for a week, I'm happy to say that if I’m going to sleep on a memory foam pillow, I want to sleep on this one.

Type: Memory foam and natural latexBest for: Combination sleepers and hot sleepersSizes: queen and king, standard and high loftTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1 yearPrice: $135 at Saatva.

Recent findings suggest that the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is sold in a standard and high loft with a breathable cotton cover that’s removable and washable. Inside the cover is a mixture of memory foam and natural latex pieces that create a comfortable and huggable pillow. The shredded foam design worked well with the cotton cover to prevent any overheating at night.

I tested the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow in a standard loft and, though I sunk slightly into it, the pillow seemed to settle to the perfect height needed to sleep comfortably on my back and stomach.

Industry observers note that while I could sleep on my side on the standard loft, I would suggest the high loft for side sleepers who need more support. This pillow gave me no reason to doubt its durability as it always returned to its shape when I got up in the morning.

It has been revealed that the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is breathable and comfortable for all sleep types. Starting at $135, it’s a luxury buy, although for Black Friday you can save when you buy a pair of pillows. Buyers also receive a 45-night trial and one-year warranty when they order this pillow.

A standard queen size Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is $135, which puts it into a premium category. Saatva rarely, if ever, includes pillows in the monthly Saatva mattress sales, but it sometimes has cut-price deals on a pair of pillows during sales events such as the Black Friday mattress sales.

In fact, the current Saatva Black Friday mattress sales have a deal where you can save up to $60 when you buy two Cloud Memory Foam Pillows at Saatva.

If this pillow was filled solely with memory foam, I’d say it was overpriced. The natural latex added to the fill and a cotton cover make the price feel more reasonable, though I think a removable fill to make the height adjustable at home would make this pillow feel like better value.

Saatva offers a 45-night trial and a one-year warranty with the purchase of this pillow. Brands like Bearaby only offer 30-day trials, so an extra 15 days is nice, until you consider the generous trial offered with the Coop Adjustable Latex Pillow — 100 nights and 5 years warranty for some of its latex pillows.

In a recent development, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow can be ordered in two sizes – queen and king – and two loft heights — standard and high. The standard loft is 4"-5" tall, while the high loft is 6"-7" in height.

This pillow has a breathable organic cotton knit cover (though it doesn’t have organic certifications) that’s removable and washable.

Recent findings suggest that despite the name of the pillow, the fill is comprised of both shredded gel-infused CertiPUR-US memory foam and natural latex foam. According to Saatva, the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is hypoallergenic.

I slept on the Helix Cooling Memory Foam Pillow for a week and performed a series of objective and subjective tests, following our pillow testing methodology.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a clear plastic bag within a cardboard box. It wasn’t vacuum sealed, meaning when I pulled it out of the plastic bag, it was ready to be slept on.

There weren’t any noticeable off-gassing smells when I pulled it from the packaging, but to be fair, I was really congested during the testing period because of hay fever.

However, when I slept on the pillow, there was an almond smell to it, which is a fairly common off-gassing scent for memory foam products.

The previous Saatva pillow I tested was too tall and didn’t have much give — which is why I breathed a sigh of relief the first time I laid my head on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

I tested a queen standard loft and discovered it to be the perfect size for someone like me who likes to sleep on her stomach, back, and side.

The shredded fill of this pillow spreads when weight is placed on it, but not enough that my head sunk down to the bed.

In a recent development, as I moved my head on the pillow, the pillow felt malleable and soft, hugging my head in a comforting way. I particularly like how this pillow feels when I’m lying on my back and stomach, as my head sinks enough to align my spine, lulling me to sleep rapidly.

Industry observers note that I can sleep on my side with the standard loft size. However, I think the high loft would be better if I was strictly a side sleeper.

When the pillow eventually breaks down, I can see myself sleeping on my side less and less with this pillow and reverting to my back or stomach. Those with broad shoulders should choose the high loft size from the get-go.

I placed a 15lb weight in the center of the pillow, and it sunk over an inch. That makes sense considering the foams inside are shredded. When I lifted the dumbbell, the pillow sprung back into shape immediately, which is a good sign of the its durability.

In a recent development, I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty when sleeping on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow, and that’s all thanks to Saatva’s temperature regulation. Memory foam is a far more heat-retaining material than natural latex, so to mitigate any overheating complications, Saatva utilized organic cotton for the cover — which is breathable — and shredded the memory foam and latex interior fill so air could weave its way through and keep my temperature neutral at night.

According to recent reports, during the beginning of testing, I was sleeping without the air-conditioner and just a fan, so it was about 75 degrees in my house when I fell asleep at night and around 70 degrees when I woke up in the morning. The fact that heat did not build up during that time was very promising, and most likely what you can expect throughout the year.

A good rule of thumb: replace your pillows every two years and keep an eye on how promptly your pillow bounces back over time.

This can be done by folding your pillow in half. A slow bounce back means the fill has worn down. Until the pillow breaks down, maintenance will ensure it lasts longer.

In a recent development, after a week of testing, I haven’t noticed any sagging or break down of the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow. The shredded nature of the memory foam and latex fill means you may not be laying your head on the same bits of foam each night, which will probably result in a longer lifespan.

The cotton cover also appears durable, and if well maintained (i.e. washed) it should hold up for at least two years. If it does break down, you could easily replace the cover, but I don’t see that happening.

Thankfully, Saatva offers a one-year limited warranty on this pillow so if you notice anything out of the ordinary, take advantage of the warranty.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that I realized how crucial it is to take care of your pillow. They easily absorb sweat, night creams, and all manner of stuff from your head and face. Maintenance ensures they last longer.

In a recent development, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is made of two parts — the cover and the fill. The cover can be removed and machine washed on cold on a delicate cycle, and either hung to dry or tumbled dry on low.

You can’t throw the memory foam and latex fill into the wash, but you can spot clean it if you need to.

Comfort is the most important thing to me when it comes to a pillow and the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow delivered.

According to recent reports, the cloud-like and huggable surface is conducive to a good night’s sleep, especially since it’s supportive enough to keep your head and spine aligned no matter what position you sleep in. If you prefer to sleep on your side, I would order the high loft option, as it’ll offer more support for a longer period of time.

The cotton cover and the shredded natural latex and memory foam fill results in a breathable design, so you won’t sleep hot or sweat at night.

During the testing period, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow bounced back rapidly, leading us to believe that it’ll last the full two years of a pillow's lifetime. Especially if you wash the cover consistently.

All in all, this supportive and huggable pillow will cradle your head and lead to a comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You overheat at night: This pillow is breathable, thanks to a cotton cover and an interior fill of shredded latex and memory foam.

Recent findings suggest that ✅ You're a combi sleeper: This pillow has the right amount of give and support for those who like to sleep on their stomach, back, and side. I suggest the high loft option for side sleepers.

✅ You like to try your pillow for a decent amount of time: Saatva lets buyers test a pillow for 45 days. If you don’t like it, Saatva will accept a return and give you a full refund.

❌ You prefer organic materials: This pillow does have some memory foam and while it’s CertiPUR-US certified, that doesn’t mean its free of toxins or VOCs, only that it’s low enough to be considered “safe.” Neither the natural latex, nor the organic cotton used in the fill and the cover are certified as organic despite claims by Saatva.

❌ You like to customize the size of your pillow: While you can order this pillow in high or low loft, unfortunately, Saatva didn’t design it so you could remove or add fill and thus adjust the height in your own home.

❌ You like a supportive, firm feel: Your head is going to sink into this soft and cloud-like pillow. For a more supportive and firm feel, try Saatva’s Down Alternative Pillow.

Sources indicate that the Helix Talalay Latex pillow is a good alternative for those who don’t like their head sinking too far into their pillow as it’s made from a single piece of foam. Expect a bouncier feel. Made with Talalay latex and perforated with holes, this pillow will help you stay cool all night long. It comes in two loft options and you can get this pillow for as little as $111, which is more affordable than the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

As the name of this pillow indicates, the Coop Sleep Good Adjustable Latex Pillow is adjustable. It's made with a blend of natural Talalay latex and microfibers, and comes with an extra bag of fill so you can add more if necessary and create the loft and feel you prefer. Our reviewer reports that the pillow is breathable and prevents heat from trapping. A 100-night trial and a 5-year warranty is worth having, too.

In a recent development, if you want buttery soft comfort for a budget price, then I reccomend the viral Squishmallows SquishPillow, which is just $29.99 in a standard size. Right now our No 1 budget pick thanks to our glowing SquishPillow review (which praised its plush comfort and reliable support), the SquishPillow comes in a medium, firm or soft.

So Is The $100 GTA 6 Ultimate Edition Actually Worth It?

💡 Key Takeaways
