📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out!
  • CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time.
  • I'll start with cargo-cgp and the upcoming documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out! This release is about making CGP easier to learn and maintain. It introduces cargo-cgp, a new tool for one of CGP's longest-standing problems: compile errors that describe the code the macros generated rather than the code you wrote. cargo-cgp explains those errors in your terms. When a provider needs a field your type lacks, for example, it can tell you which field to add, and the expanded documentation explains why the provider needs it. Later, as your application grows, the new namespaces let you choose the providers for a whole group of components in one wiring entry.

CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time. It is an ordinary library on stable Rust: applications select providers through wiring that resolves to static calls, and you can adopt it one component at a time. The Overview explains the model.

I'll start with cargo-cgp and the upcoming documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application. The namespace walkthrough is the longest part, so you can read the tooling and documentation news on their own if you prefer. Allow about 35 minutes for the full post, including the code, or jump to the section you need:.

Since CGP began, verbose and confusing compiler errors have been one of the largest obstacles to adopting it. Leave out a field or a component binding, and the error message can name a generated trait or show a field name encoded as a Rust type. The compiler checks the Rust produced by macro expansion, so its explanation can be far removed from the code where we made the mistake.

Recent findings suggest that for a newcomer, that can mean learning advanced Rust traits and generics, along with CGP's internals, just to diagnose a small mistake. You might understand the program you are trying to write and still have little idea why it does not compile. Because the difficulty lies in how the compiler reports the expanded code, better syntax alone cannot address it.

It has been revealed that so I built cargo-cgp v0.1.0, CGP's new error toolchain, to report those errors in terms of the code you wrote. cargo cgp check checks CGP code and explains a missing dependency through the fields, components, and providers involved, leading with the root cause. It does not yet reshape every class of error, though, so some still reach you in the compiler's own words. When you want to look deeper, cargo cgp expand highlights the Rust that the macros generated.

Let's try it on a small mistake from the area-calculation tutorial. We have an area provider that multiplies width by height, and a Rectangle that supplies only width. Here, the rectangle itself is the context: it is the value the operation acts on, and its fields supply the provider's inputs.

Save this library example as src/lib.rs in a Cargo package using cgp = "0.8.0":.

Industry observers note that the table selects RectangleArea, whose #[implicit] arguments read the rectangle's fields. Because we used delegate_and_check_components!, the compiler checks those dependencies at the wiring entry. Run cargo cgp check, and it points to the field we forgot:.

The help line gives us the edit, height: f64. To see why the provider needs it, the dependency tree takes us back through RectangleArea to the area operation. For comparison, plain cargo check describes the same mistake through generated traits and a nested Symbol type:.

Following that suggestion, we add the missing field:.

The wiring check now passes, and the provider can read both fields to calculate the area. Fixing the mistake did not require decoding the type-level spelling of height.

Recent findings suggest that to produce this explanation, cargo-cgp wraps a nightly compiler and uses the Rust compiler's API to inspect the failed dependencies. It can follow their chain using information that would be difficult to recover from the printed diagnostic alone. That access is why the tool has its own compiler-linked driver.

With cargo and rustup available, you can install the tool and set up its compiler-linked driver, then check your own project. The install needs Rust 1.96 or newer, and the tool is tested on Linux only so far:.

It has been revealed that cargo cgp setup installs the tool's pinned nightly and builds the matching driver. That nightly runs only cargo-cgp's checks, so your application keeps its normal toolchain for ordinary cargo builds. CGP itself still compiles on stable Rust, and you can use it without installing cargo-cgp at all.

Use plain cargo to build, run, and test applications. cargo-cgp supplies check for diagnostics and expand for reading the Rust generated by macros, with CGP's type-level constructs restored to readable notation. The installation guide covers setup, updates, and the Nix alternative, and the cargo-cgp v0.1.0 release notes list what this first release supports.

Industry observers note that A release post can show you an interesting feature and still leave you unsure how to use it in your own program. For too long, CGP left readers in that position. Most explanations lived in blog posts like this one, with each post introducing features as they arrived. There was little room to explain every construct or give readers a complete account of how the pieces fit together.

CGP is a side project, and finding the time to fill those gaps has been difficult. Writing a comparable body of documentation entirely by hand would likely take me months of full-time work. I do not expect to have that time in the near future, and waiting would leave readers facing the same gaps.

Industry observers note that advances in AI and agentic coding made it practical to take on that work. Agents, primarily Claude Code, wrote much of the newly introduced documentation under my direction, over many iterations of planning and revision. If a blog post leaves you wanting more detail, you can now turn to:.

Across more than 360 pages, the website now contains roughly 365,000 words of documentation prose, excluding code blocks and the mirrored skill files. At 300 words per printed page, that would be about 1,200 pages before code listings.

I understand why readers may be skeptical of AI-written explanations. A word count indicates little about their usefulness, and I would not expect a one-shot prompt to produce useful material at this scale. The planning, source checks, and repeated revisions are essential to the quality I am aiming for. I encourage you to read the pages and tell me where an explanation is vague, incorrect, or reads like generic AI output.

Industry observers note that I direct the work, set the rules, and choose what gets documented. The process starts with the knowledge base, where agents record how CGP works and check claims about syntax and macro expansions against the implementation, tests, and expansion snapshots. That account becomes the basis for the website pages, which agents write and revise against the project's writing guides.

In a recent development, when a page needs an upgrade, the agent can pick up from the same record. That saves me time because each revision starts from what the record already holds about CGP. The knowledge-base overview explains how the record supports the project.

I review the pages myself, though not all in the same depth. I read in full every page that explains CGP's ideas or the decisions behind its design, which includes the Concepts pages and the blog posts. The reference pages for individual constructs follow their writing guides, and I spot-check them. But neither kind of review catches everything. Like the source checks, it can miss mistakes, so the knowledge base can still contain errors. I remain responsible for what the project publishes.

According to recent reports, I would like to explore the methodology further in a dedicated follow-up post. For now, How CGP's Documentation Is Written explains the process and where its checks stop. The AI disclosure describes who writes and reviews the documentation, tooling, and core library.

If you already work with an AI assistant, try exploring a small CGP example together. With the /cgp skill loaded, you can ask it to explain an unfamiliar wiring entry, trace which provider a method uses, or help investigate a compiler error. This gives you a way to explore the internal details as they become relevant, with explanations suited to your Rust experience.

Industry observers note that the skill gives the assistant a condensed guide to current CGP: the consumer/provider model, wiring, dependency declarations, and debugging with cargo-cgp. It can help the assistant investigate macro expansions and guide you through installing and using the checker. For deeper questions, it can consult the fuller knowledge-base record.

Before it works on your code, the skill checks which cgp release your project uses and tells you when that differs from the release it describes. You still need to review and verify the assistant's suggested code. The installation page explains how to install the skill in your agent, and Using the Knowledge Base with Your Agent covers deeper investigation. Neither is required to use CGP.

The release also introduces namespaces, for grouping components as an application grows.

According to recent reports, when an application has only a few components, writing out its delegate_components! table is straightforward. Each time we split behavior into another component, though, we add a routing entry. Eventually, someone opening the application has to sort through a long list of bindings before they can see which ones belong together. The implementations have become more reusable, but the configuration has become harder to follow.

I have tried a few ways to address this difficulty. Provider bundles collect implementations, but applications still have to list the components they forward to each bundle. The earlier preset system reduced some repetition too, with limitations I will return to below.

With namespaces, we can now give those groups names and select their implementations together. I'll work through a social-media application whose production and test configurations share a PostgreSQL-backed core but use different content filters. By the end, that difference will be visible in one wiring entry.

Sources indicate that if you have already maintained a large wiring table, you may prefer to jump to the namespace syntax or the migration guide. Otherwise, let's start with the small application and see how its wiring grows.

Sources indicate that suppose we are building a social-media service that manages users and posts. We need a database handle and a place to choose the implementations the service uses, so our context will represent the application. This is a different role from the earlier Rectangle, where the context was the data being operated on.

The snippets illustrate wiring rather than a complete web service. They assume use cgp::prelude::*; and omit domain type declarations and database query bodies. The web-app walkthrough follows the same example, and its compiling source uses placeholder database operations.

Our service starts with one manager trait for users and another for posts.

In a recent development, the methods describe what the service can do. Adding #[cgp_component] lets us write their implementations separately from the application that uses them: it generates a provider trait such as UserManager and a wiring key such as UserManagerComponent. The application will choose a provider through that key.

Recent findings suggest that choosing a manager provider chooses all its methods together. A component can hold several methods, associated types, and constants, just like an ordinary trait, and grouping the user operations keeps this first version simple. As the service grows, we will see where choosing those methods together becomes inconvenient.

For the PostgreSQL implementations, each method declares the database handle it needs as an implicit argument. The providers can then work with any application supplying that dependency:.

Any context with the required PostgreSQL database field can reuse these providers. If we wanted a SQLite-backed application, we could write SqliteUserManager and SqlitePostManager against the same interfaces and select those instead.

For our production application, we supply the database field and choose the PostgreSQL managers:.

In a recent development, both managers share one dependency: the database field that #[derive(HasField)] makes available to their implicit arguments. The combined delegation-and-check macro verifies that ProductionApp can use the selected providers. For now, those two entries cover all the user and post operations.

Now suppose the service needs to reject censored usernames and spam posts. Before inserting a user or a post, its manager must consult a filter. We can add a component for each check and declare the manager's dependency on its consumer trait with #[uses]:.

It has been revealed that each manager compares its filter's score with a rejection threshold before writing to the database. The #[uses] attribute declares the upcoming trait dependency, while #[implicit] database still supplies the database handle. The remaining manager methods are omitted here.

Recent findings suggest that in production, filtering might involve an AI model or a cloud service. We would rather not make those calls every time we test the rest of the application. A deterministic string-matching filter lets tests run more swiftly while keeping the same PostgreSQL managers:.

Both contexts supply the database field and select the same managers. Only the filter entries differ, so tests can exercise the database implementations with deterministic filtering.

The wiring has grown along with the dependency tree. Each context now has four entries, so the two contexts together already have eight to keep in step, even in this small service.

In a recent development, adding CanCensorUsername to the user manager looked straightforward. But that bound belongs to the whole PostgresUserManager implementation, so even get_user now requires a context with a censor. Retrieving a user never runs the filter. The dependency arrives because retrieval and creation share a provider. The post manager has the same problem with spam detection, and every unrelated dependency we add makes the managers harder to maintain and test.

As we add operations, the domain boundaries become less obvious too. get_user_profile_picture might fit in the user manager, but it could need an entirely different set of dependencies. get_user_posts concerns both users and posts. Naming a manager after an entity does not settle which operations are useful to group together.

There is also a reason to keep the caller's interface narrow. Deleting a user is destructive, and we may not want every piece of code that works with users to be able to do it. Yet if we added delete_user to the manager, even generic code that only retrieves users would gain access to deletion. Giving retrieval its own trait lets that code ask for exactly the operation it needs, and nothing more.

In a recent development, that points to a simple but powerful pattern that CGP makes practical: splitting each manager into fine-grained traits, each holding one operation or a few closely related ones. Each provider can then declare only the dependencies it uses. For the user operations, that gives us:.

The user-creation provider needs the censor, while the getter needs only the database:.

Sources indicate that getUserWithPostgres can be used with a database alone, while CreateUserWithPostgres keeps its censor dependency. A caller bounded by CanGetUser can retrieve people without depending on creation or deletion. The same split gives us separate post-creation, retrieval, revision, and deletion components.

Industry observers note that splitting the components solved the getter's problem, but CreateUserWithPostgres still does two jobs: it checks the username, then inserts the user into PostgreSQL. Only the insert has anything to do with the database. If we added a provider for SQLite, it would have to repeat the same check. Because creation now has a component of its own, we can move the check into a wrapper instead, and apply it to whichever user-creation provider we choose:.

Industry observers note that the wrapper rejects censored names, then hands an allowed request to InnerCreator::create_user. Its #[use_provider] attribute requires that inner provider to support user creation for the same context. Because it takes another provider as a parameter, we call FilterCensoredUsername a higher-order provider.

Industry observers note that createUserWithPostgres can now focus on constructing the SQL insert query. When wiring the application, we can select it directly or add filtering with FilterCensoredUsername. A local-first application could instead select FilterCensoredUsername and reuse the same filter. Changing the database would not require copying the username check.

In a recent development, filterSpamMessage applies the same separation to post creation. It uses CanDetectSpamMessage to reject spam, then forwards an allowed post to its inner PostCreator. The wiring can therefore choose FilterSpamMessage independently of the database provider's implementation.

Industry observers note that with dependencies isolated and filters reusable, the individual providers are easier to work with. The production wiring, however, now has to select seven CRUD operations and two filters:.

In a recent development, splitting the managers took our wiring table from four entries to nine, and a real application might have dozens or hundreds. Imagine opening that table for the first time. To learn how the application handles users, you have to pick the user bindings out of the list, and everything else reads as noise that hides what ProductionApp actually does. The application then looks far more complex than it is, which is one reason long wiring tables have made CGP harder to adopt.

It has been revealed that the table highlights us too much at once. If we break it into smaller groups, a reader can take the wiring one piece at a time, so let's start by collecting the user bindings into a provider bundle of their own:.

In a recent development, with new PostgresUserComponents, we declare an aggregate provider: its table delegates each operation to another provider. A reader can examine the user wiring on its own, without the post operations and filters alongside it. We can collect those into PostgresPostComponents and AiContentFilterComponents in the same way.

Back in the application, we forward the components to their bundles using array keys:.

The bundles make each group easier to read, but they do not shorten what the application has to list. Its table still names all nine components, now split across three lists, and each list repeats the keys its bundle already holds. So adding a user operation takes two edits: one to the user bundle, and another to every application that delegates to it. In a large codebase, that second edit could mean many places. We would rather tell the application to use PostgresUserComponents for “all user components,” but that group has no name we can wire.

Ideally, the configuration would say something like this, with a key for each group:.

According to recent reports, the ??? keys are the hard part. Each entry in the table becomes a trait implementation for one key, so UserCreatorComponent: … gives the application one implementation that answers lookups for user creation. A key that stood for all user components would need to produce one implementation per component in the group, and Rust's trait system has no way to expand a single entry like that. So CGP needs another way to recognize a group: either its own lookup rules, or a macro that expands the group into its keys. Namespaces take the first route, but the macro route is worth a look first.

Industry observers note that one possibility would be a helper macro that supplied the list of keys for each group. That would let us write a hypothetical table like this:.

It has been revealed that here, all_user_components!() would expand to [UserCreatorComponent, UserGetterComponent, UserUpdaterComponent], with corresponding lists for posts and filters. Like the ??? keys above, these helpers are pseudocode rather than supported syntax.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, this runs into the order in which Rust expands macros. Rust expands them lazily, from the outside in, so delegate_components! runs first and receives all_user_components!() as literal tokens. At that point the helper has not expanded, and the component list does not exist yet. The table would need eager expansion, where a macro expands the macros inside its input before reading it, and stable Rust offers no way for a macro to do that. Even if it did, CGP would still have to generate helpers like all_user_components! and export them so that their names and imports keep working in other crates, and Rust's macro system has limited support for that.

My earlier preset system tried to solve the same problem, but it supported only a hierarchy like single inheritance. A context could inherit one preset, such as a user preset, and Rust's coherence restrictions then stopped it from also inheriting an independent post preset. I also experimented with combining several presets through macros, but the lack of eager macro expansion, together with the way imports and aliases resolve inside macro output, made that approach tedious to use.

According to recent reports, those attempts helped clarify what I wanted from the feature: an application should be able to name a group and choose its implementation bundle without enumerating every key. In v0.8.0, namespaces express that choice through trait resolution and paths. Existing preset users can find the conversion in the migration section.

We can now replace the ??? keys with paths that name the user, post, and content-filter groups. With the component prefixes registered, our application table becomes:.

The namespace DefaultNamespace; statement connects these paths to our components. Each component registers a route in the built-in DefaultNamespace, as we will do in a moment with #[prefix], and the statement tells the table to follow those routes. Namespaces are opt-in, so without this statement the table ignores the registered routes. A lookup for UserCreatorComponent, for example, follows a route that begins with @app.core.user, so it reaches the entry that selects PostgresUserComponents. Adding another user operation to the user group therefore leaves this table unchanged. The individual bindings still live in the bundles, while the application chooses only which groups it uses. Later, we will also define a namespace of our own.

To make this work, we give each component a prefix using #[prefix]. For CanCreateUser, we register @app.core.user in the built-in DefaultNamespace:.

It has been revealed that CGP appends the component marker to this prefix. Once a context joins the namespace, a lookup for UserCreatorComponent follows the route to @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent.

Recent findings suggest that the getter and updater belong to that group too, so we register them under the same prefix. For the getter, that means:.

Post operations get their own @app.core.post prefix:.

It has been revealed that finally, the filter components register under @app.extra.content_filter, also in DefaultNamespace. These registrations name the groups without choosing any providers for them. That choice stays with each application, so production, tests, and a SQLite variant can share the same routes and still select different bundles.

Production and tests both use the PostgreSQL user and post operations. Rather than select those bundles separately in each application, we can collect them under their shared parent, @app.core. The paths are hierarchical: @app.core.user sits under @app.core, which sits under @app. An intermediate bundle can therefore gather the core operations, while another gathers the extras:.

Recent findings suggest that notice that these intermediate bundles also join DefaultNamespace. When a lookup reaches a bundle, it receives the bare component key, and the namespace statement redirects that key to the paths in the bundle's own table. Our earlier leaf bundles use bare component names already, so they do not need that statement.

The production configuration now selects two groups:.

A single entry for @app.core now covers both core groups. Because paths are hierarchical, it matches every route beneath that prefix, so user and post lookups both reach it, and so would a core group we add later. Take UserCreatorComponent again. Its route, @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent, begins with @app.core, so ProductionApp forwards the lookup to PostgresCoreComponents. Inside that bundle, the namespace statement routes the component a second time, which brings it to the @app.core.user entry and on to PostgresUserComponents.

Recent findings suggest that for testing, the core stays the same. Only the extras entry changes, selecting DummyExtraComponents for deterministic filtering:.

For a local configuration, we could make the other choice: keep the production filters and select a SQLite-backed core:.

Recent findings suggest that in each case, one entry tells us how the configuration differs from production. TestApp changes the extras, while LocalApp changes the core. With flat tables, we would have to compare the individual component entries, perhaps written in different orders, to reach the same conclusion. We can now read those decisions directly from the wiring.

The selected providers still need their dependencies. Each context must supply the required fields and other traits, and the hypothetical SQLite core would need its corresponding database handle.

Will these providers work together? A delegate_components! block can compile before Rust has checked the providers' dependencies. We can ask Rust to check them now with check_components!, naming the components we need on the concrete application.

Industry observers note that apply the same nine-component check to TestApp and any local variant. Earlier stages need checks matching their components: before splitting the managers, for example, check UserManagerComponent and PostManagerComponent.

In a recent development, the check lists the individual operations, even though the wiring now routes them in groups. A group entry only says where a lookup goes, so the check confirms that every operation we rely on actually resolves. Run it on the real application context, which supplies the database field and the other dependencies. An aggregate provider is only a bundle of implementations, so checking a bundle as if it were the application would ask it for dependencies that only the context can supply.

Sources indicate that the namespace documentation explains the lookup model, and the delegate_components! reference covers the path syntax.

So far, we have organized the wiring around choices we might want to change: PostgreSQL or SQLite, production or test filters. Bundles work well for that arrangement. We could add a PostgresWithLoggingCoreComponents variant, for example, and select the logging-backed core in the same place.

But an application starting out with PostgreSQL may have little reason to define interchangeable database bundles yet. Early in a project, developers often prefer one implementation per feature, tied to its interface on purpose, because that keeps the application easy to reason about. If several contexts should always use the same user and post implementations, having each one select those bundles repeats a choice that never varies. We can instead record those choices once in a namespace and leave only the varying parts to each context. These are default implementations.

I see defaults as a way to adopt CGP gradually. Ordinary traits may already be enough for a single-crate application with one implementation of each operation. If that application later needs more modularity, it can move code into CGP components and record its initial provider choices as defaults. Bundles can follow when there are useful groups to swap.

In a recent development, let's keep the routes we already registered in DefaultNamespace and define a configuration namespace that inherits them using the latest cgp_namespace! macro:.

DefaultAppComponents starts with the prefixes and any default bindings supplied by its parent. We can add our application-specific choices here without changing what other namespaces select. Every context that joins this configuration namespace will share those choices.

Recent findings suggest that for a simple provider, we can place its binding beside its implementation. Add #[default_impl] to our earlier GetUserWithPostgres definition:.

The implementation now declares that DefaultAppComponents uses it at @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent. If we prefer to collect the bindings in one place, we can write the same choice in the namespace body instead:.

These are alternative ways to register the same binding, so writing both would create a conflict. The namespace body looks like a delegate_components! table, but its choices apply to every context that joins the namespace. We bind the provider at the full path because the bare key is already taken. The route inherited from DefaultNamespace uses UserGetterComponent to send lookups on to @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent, so a second entry for the bare key would conflict with it.

These defaults are fixed choices. Once the namespace binds a provider, a joining context or inheriting namespace cannot override it, even with a more specific entry. A context also cannot disable just one default while retaining the rest of that namespace. So a choice that should vary between contexts belongs on a path the namespace leaves open, as we will do with the filters below.

There is also a constraint on where we write the registration. With a prefixed path, the binding must live in the crate that owns the namespace, here DefaultAppComponents. The path expands to CGP's PathCons type, and owning a component marker nested inside that type does not satisfy Rust's orphan rules. An unprefixed local component marker has different ownership rules, covered by the #[default_impl] reference.

It has been revealed that filterCensoredUsername is generic over its inner provider. For this configuration, we want to choose both the wrapper and its PostgreSQL implementation. We can assemble that complete provider choice directly in the namespace body:.

After we bind the remaining user and post providers in the same way, the application only needs to choose its filters. For this example, our production wiring then becomes:.

Every context that joins DefaultAppComponents gets its user and post providers from it. We left the filter path open so a test context can select DummyContentFilterComponents there instead.

We kept the prefixes in DefaultNamespace and the provider choices in DefaultAppComponents for a reason. Another configuration, such as a SQLite one, can then inherit the same routes without also inheriting PostgreSQL choices it could not override. So the routes belong in a base namespace, and the fixed choices in a configuration namespace that inherits it.

If we later need to replace one of these fixed defaults, we choose a namespace that leaves its destination open. We could return to the base DefaultNamespace and supply the required bindings explicitly, as in the earlier bundle examples.

While the application lives in one crate, #[default_impl] conveniently keeps each binding beside its implementation. Once providers move into crates of their own, that attribute would sit in a crate that does not own the namespace, which the ownership rule above forbids. So we move the bindings into the configuration namespace's body instead, and the namespace's crate assembles the providers from there.

According to recent reports, there is room to start with direct wiring, share fixed choices through defaults, and introduce interchangeable bundles as the application needs them. I would choose whichever arrangement makes the current decisions easiest to see, rather than build the full hierarchy in anticipation of future growth.

Namespaces are the largest change, but several smaller additions also make CGP easier to write, read, and use in more kinds of crates. You can use these without following the full application refactoring above:.

For the smaller changes, such as clearer errors from the handler macros and the restrictions this release lifts, see the v0.8.0 release notes.

Upgrading from v0.7.0 needs source changes. The largest is the removal of presets, which namespaces replace in this release, and most applications will also need explicit imports for items that used to come from the prelude. The v0.8.0 release notes list every change, with the upgrade steps in order.

It has been revealed that two projects built with CGP move to v0.8.0 at the same time. cgp-serde 0.3.0 can now serialize and deserialize enums, and Hypershell 0.2.0 assembles its language from a namespace instead of presets. If your code builds on either, the cgp-serde v0.3.0 and Hypershell v0.2.0 release notes give the upgrade steps.

Recent findings suggest that the preset system described earlier is removed in v0.8.0. Its shared provider choices can become namespace bindings, while groups that need to remain interchangeable can become aggregate providers selected through paths.

Recent findings suggest that the following v0.7.0 example defines a preset and inherits it into a context. This is old syntax and does not compile with v0.8.0:.

In a recent development, A configuration namespace can preserve the preset's fixed user-provider choices. Register the user components under @app.core.user in DefaultNamespace, using the #[prefix(... in DefaultNamespace)] attributes shown earlier. Then replace the preset with this namespace:.

According to recent reports, the migrated context must also supply the censor required by its creation wrapper. Register UsernameCensor under @app.extra.content_filter in DefaultNamespace. With the user components and filter registered, replace the inheritance attribute with explicit delegation on the context:.

The example above deliberately checks only the migrated user group and its filter. Add the post operations and any other dependencies your application uses.

It has been revealed that an aggregate provider keeps the user-provider group interchangeable. If configurations need that variation, retain PostgresUserComponents using delegate_components! { fresh PostgresUserComponents { ... } } and select it with @app.core.user: PostgresUserComponents, as in the main walkthrough. Choose between this configurable bundle arrangement and the fixed namespace bindings above according to what should vary.

The removed preset constructs and their replacements are:.

Sources indicate that cgp::prelude now exports only the names CGP code usually writes: the macros, the derives, PhantomData, and a few traits and providers such as HasErrorType, CanRaiseError, UseType, and DefaultNamespace. The code the macros generate reaches CGP's items through a separate cgp::macro_prelude, so the prelude no longer has to carry those items. If your code names one of the dropped items through the glob import, the compiler reports that it cannot find it, and you import it from its module:.

The dropped names come from these modules:.

A derive does not need its trait imported, so #[derive(HasField)] still works through the prelude, while a HasField bound or a .get_field() call needs the import. A provider for a handler trait such as Computer imports its key, ComputerComponent, beside the trait, because the provider's header names the key, as Other improvements describes.

Industry observers note that raw compiler output changes slightly as a result. Where v0.7.0 printed a type such as cgp::prelude::Chars, the compiler can now print cgp::macro_prelude::Chars, as in the cargo check comparison above.

Sources indicate that the type-level types also lose their Greek-letter names. v0.7.0 declared them as π, ε, σ, θ, ζ, ψ, δ, and ω, with Cons, Nil, Either, Void, Chars, Symbol, Index, and Field as aliases, and the prelude exported both spellings. Only the English names remain, so code that wrote a Greek name switches to the English one, imported from cgp::core::field::types. Raw compiler output changes with them, printing Cons<…> and Chars<…> where v0.7.0 printed π<…> and ζ<…>.

According to recent reports, the default features of cgp are now empty, so the library builds without std or an allocator. In v0.7.0, the defaults turned on DebugError and DisplayError, the error providers that format an error into a String. If your wiring uses either, turn on the alloc feature:.

The associated-type separator in #[use_type] changes from :: to .:.

Sources indicate that equality imports use the new separator too. Write #[use_type(HasErrorType.{Error = AppError})]. An import from another context changes shape as well, with the context named after in: #[use_type(@Types::HasScalarType::Scalar)] becomes #[use_type(HasScalarType.Scalar in Types)]. The #[use_type] reference covers each form.

A component that generates a UseDelegate dispatcher moves the derive_delegate key of #[cgp_component] into an attribute of its own, one per dispatcher:.

A latest component does not need either form, because the open statement from Other improvements dispatches it per type.

The extra-feature macro crates are renamed from cgp-extra-macro and cgp-extra-macro-lib to cgp-macro-extra and cgp-macro-extra-lib. Patch direct dependencies on those crates. Imports through cgp::prelude keep their names.

Self-contained handler-macro expansions may leave imports unused. Remove imports the compiler reports when they existed only for the old expansion.

#[cgp_auto_dispatch] rejects attribute arguments and typed receivers such as self: Box. It previously ignored the arguments or miscompiled those receivers.

The new Struct! and Enum! prelude exports can make a macro name ambiguous. Qualify the call if another glob import provides the same name.

DelegateComponent, IsProviderFor, HasField, and HasFieldMut no longer carry custom #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] messages. Plain cargo check now reports an unmet bound on them in the compiler's own wording, and cargo cgp check rewrites those errors into its own summary. If a test compares compiler output, as a UI test does, patch the messages it expects.

cgp-error-eyre enables eyre's automatic default-handler installation and tracks the caller of raise_error and wrap_error.

cgp-error-std changes how wrapped errors are displayed. Ordinary Display prints only the outer detail, while alternate Display and Debug include the chain. This avoids duplicated sources when a reporter walks source() itself. Enhancement output assertions that depend on the old formatting.

According to recent reports, the minimum anyhow and eyre dependencies rise to 1.0.104 and 0.6.14 respectively. The backend READMEs in the CGP repository describe their use.

We started with two manager choices and ended with applications that could share a core, change their filters, or use a different database. Namespaces let the top-level wiring express those choices even as we split the implementations into smaller pieces. I hope that makes similar refactorings easier to follow in your own projects, with cargo-cgp and the new documentation there to help when something is unclear.

CGP still takes time to learn. Its ecosystem is small, and I still have work to do on the tooling and documentation. My suggestion is to try it on one problem you already have. If you already use CGP, try grouping one area of your wiring while keeping its component checks in place. If you are new to CGP, the Quickstart provides a smaller starting point.

I would appreciate hearing where you still struggle to trace an implementation, understand a diagnostic, or follow an explanation. Those examples will help me decide what to improve next. You can share them in GitHub Discussions. Thank you for reading and trying CGP.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that luckily, the code can be found nearby, but it's not as clear as some of the other safe codes in GTA 6.
  • Here's what the Declasse Vamos code is in GTA 6, and how to find it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Declasse Vamos is a car that you can steal for Moses in Grand Theft Auto 6. However, when you find the Declasse Vamos, you realize that it's locked away inside a garage, and you need to find the door code to get to it.

It has been revealed that luckily, the code can be found nearby, but it's not as clear as some of the other safe codes in GTA 6. You won't find any notes that explicitly tell you what the code is, but if you pay close attention to your surroundings, you'll find a common number that just so happens to be the code.

Here's what the Declasse Vamos code is in GTA 6, and how to find it.

According to recent reports, before you can steal the Declasse Vamos for Moses, you need to first steal the initial three cars that he asks you to look out for. Then, Moses will eventually hit you up with more vehicles to steal, which will include the souped-up Declasse Vamos. The Declasse Vamos is the car that's located at the eastern edge of Grayson, in Lummox County.

The Declasse Vamos you need to steal for Moses is locked in the standalone garage beside the house. On the west side of the garage, you'll find a door and a keypad that you need a four-digit code for.

To find the code, you need to go inside the house to the west of the garage, but it's vital to note that there are a few people inside. In our experience, there was a person sleeping in the living room and a few people talking on the back porch. You can either go guns a-blazing or sneak in.

Industry observers note that there isn't a note that will explicitly tell you "this is the code for the garage." Instead, you need to look for a four-digit number that could be the code. Luckily, there's one plastered across the walls of the house: 2727.

The keypad code for the garage is 2-7-2-7. Input the code and the door to the garage will unlock. Head inside, and make sure to open the garage door by pressing the button to its right.

From here, you're free to get into the car and drive off. The people inside the house will notice that you're stealing their car and try to shoot you, but if you drive off fast enough, they won't be following you for long. Take the car back to Moses, and he'll pay you $4,135 dollars.

In a recent development, if you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. Check out our GTA 6 beginner guide to get a grasp of the basics and our tips for what to do first, recommendations for the best ways to make money fast, and an explainer for how to keep stolen weapons and cars to make the most of your free time.

Sources indicate that our selection of GTA 6 guides includes help for things like how to steal the Phoenix in "Unwanted Attention" and whether you should defuse Mandy, too. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system.
  • In a recent development, while we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Industry observers note that most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-notable director.

In a recent development, while we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

Sources indicate that jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

According to recent reports, "The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

"Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole Fresh World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing.".

It has been revealed that the pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

Recent findings suggest that before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

That sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French Upcoming Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

Their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their organization AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a significant idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

It has been revealed that that approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

Marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

It has been revealed that that set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

That made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Industry observers note that phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

According to recent reports, the duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Industry observers note that their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

According to recent reports, lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that highlighted off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

Industry observers note that but what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting significant. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

Recent findings suggest that the sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

In a recent development, widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in Upcoming York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

The brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

Few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production manufacturer, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

According to recent reports, that led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

Joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" announced a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

Industry observers note that working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Big Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

It has been revealed that after 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they remarked they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix plans to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

The original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that roger Ebert wasn't as effusive about Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings" films as many other critics. For reference, Ebert gave "Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Two Towers" three stars (out of four) and then "Return of the King" three and a half.

According to recent reports, "A true visualization of [J.R.R.] Tolkien's Middle-earth it is not," wrote Ebert of Jackson's "Fellowship," arguing it "adds up to more of a sword and sorcery epic" that loses the "innocence" of the books. Though, Ebert conceded in that review that "That 'Fellowship of the Ring' doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours.".

Ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R. Tolkien." However, he praised "Return of the King" as a strong conclusion which solidified the trilogy as "a work of bold ambition at a time of cinematic timidity," even if he felt the film and trilogy fell "a little shy of greatness.".

Sources indicate that but you know what fantasy movie Ebert did love? 2007's "The Golden Compass," adapted from Philip Pullman's "His Dark Materials" novels. It's set in an alternate world where a piece of every person's soul exists in the form of an animal, called a dæmon. British orphan Lyra Belacqua (Dakota Blue Richards) embarks on a quest to rescue a friend and stumbles onto a much more cosmic struggle. Ebert gave it four stars, writing:.

"'The Golden Compass' is a darker, deeper fantasy epic than the 'Rings' trilogy, 'The Chronicles of Narnia' or the 'Potter' films. It springs from the same British world of quasi-philosophical magic, but creates more complex villains and poses more intriguing questions.".

While most would disagree with Ebert's quality assessment, he's onto something, as "Golden Compass" invites "Lord of the Rings" comparisons.

Sources indicate that "The Golden Compass" was produced by New Line Cinema, the same production organization behind "The Lord of the Rings," and it's clear the studio was hoping to repeat its previous success. "The Golden Compass" even features two important "Rings" alums: Ian McKellen (Gandalf) as the voice of polar bear king Iorek Byrnison, and Christopher Lee (the corrupted wizard Saruman) as a leader of the Magisterium, the Church of Lyra's world. It was reported in 2007 both actors were cast at New Line's behest.

But quite the contrary, "The Golden Compass" under-performed ($372 million in theaters against a $180 million budget), and sequels were never made. "The Golden Compass" even contributed to the end of Latest Line as an independent studio, as it was folded into Warner Bros. in 2008. Not helping the movie's financials was a religious backlash. The Magisterium allegorically represents all authoritarian religions but especially the Catholic Church, and "The Golden Compass" was in turn condemned by the Vatican.

In a recent development, "The Golden Compass" didn't win over fans of its source novel, either, due to abundant changes. The movie cuts out the book's entire ending, which directly sets up the sequel, "The Subtle Knife." But the attacks on religion? Those are taken right from the book. Philip Pullman is an atheist, and "His Dark Materials" is his rebuttal to the Christian-themed British fantasies of J.R.R. Tolkien and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis, particularly the latter as both stories are about children traveling to different worlds. (Though Tolkien, for what it's worth, is stated to have disliked "Narnia.").

"I cordially dislike allegory," Tolkien once famously claimed, believing it robs readers the freedom to interpret a work. For decades, stated readers have since read into the influence of Tolkien's Catholic faith on his Middle-earth stories.

Sauron and his ring are a Luciferian conception of evil: A fallen angel who rules a fiery, molten realm and whose darkness spreads as temptation. J. R. R. Tolkien's villain is the Devil, Philip Pullman's is the Church.

In a recent development, frodo carrying the ring echoes Christ carrying his own cross to Golgotha and, in turn, the metaphorical crosses that all of Christ's followers carry. "The Chronicles of Narnia," meanwhile, features talking lion Aslan as a direct allegory for the Christian God, Christ-like sacrifice and resurrection included.

In "His Dark Materials," the Magisterium worships "the Authority," a name suggesting an "authority" is all that organized religion is. The Authority is also a liar: He is not the creator of the universe, merely the first "angel" who came into being. The weak and withered "god" eventually crumbles into dust, as if humanity has no more use for him. The very last dialogue of the trilogy is Lyra endeavoring to build a "Republic of Heaven" on Earth.

Yet, circling back to Roger Ebert, he disputed the anti-religious reading of the "Golden Compass" movie, arguing it reworks the Magisterium into a more purely political villain, "a Soviet dictatorship or Major Brother." He specifically praised the film's themes as "murky," compared to Pullman's blatant allegory for the death of God, and affirmed that "the controversy surrounding ['The Golden Compass'] obscures its function as a splendid entertainment.".

Amusingly, Ebert championed the movie for the same reasons many "His Dark Materials" fans rejected it. Toning down the anti-religion elements did not spare the movie the Church's wrath, either. One can only wonder what Ebert would have thought of the eventual "His Dark Materials" TV series that adapted Pullman's story to book fans' delight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aqara has unveiled the global launch of six upcoming smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the organization describes as “spatial intelligence.”.

The newly introduced lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization ….

All of the new products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the latest products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Industry observers note that its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

Sources indicate that you might initially struggle to spot the new products in the firm’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

In a recent development, pricing ranges from $24 for upcoming light bulbs through to $320 for the 100-foot-long permanent outdoor rope lights. You can find all the new products here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though. GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

[Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.].

Update (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

Sources indicate that if you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a fresh Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

You won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a new Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

To activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

Note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ] More information about the Gnupg-announce mailing list.

It has been revealed that messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ] Hello! We are pleased to announce the availability of a latest GPGME release: version 2.3.1. This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in all prior versions. We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME. Description =========== By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is possible to trigger a double free. This double free can be used exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data. Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't be ruled out. Thus an immediate update is highly suggested. Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557) The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975. This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed by GitLab on 2026-11-12. Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20. The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the status lines and key listings from gpg. Initially a buffer of 1024 bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required. When reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the function. Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to the freed memory. Eventually the context is released and the memory freed a second time. Due to other allocations in between the common double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered. Impact ====== All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected. Examples of software using GPGME are - Gpg4win - GnuPG Desktop - GnuPG VS-Desktop - Most mail clients - Many XMPP clients - Samba - Flatpack Solution ======== Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1. If you need a DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version. For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME 2.3.1. If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to very old versions. There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT. Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19) ================================================ [compared to version 2.2.0] * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM. Add mappings for algos used bei backends. [rMa85fa49236] * Fix a double free in the status line read code. [T8557,CVE-2026-129975] * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ GPGME_PK_DLTHM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLKEM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLDSA NEW. Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427 Getting the Software ==================== Please follow the instructions found at or read on: The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature are available here: https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k) https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is attached. Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. Debian Packages =============== We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants. See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch to other distros/releases. Windows Installer ================= A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer, including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF reader has also been released. Head over to https://gpg4win.org/ Checking the Integrity ====================== See https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html The checksum for gpgme is: 1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 *Thank you all* Your GnuPG hackers p.s. This is an announcement only mailing list. Please send replies only to the gnupg-customers at gnupg.org mailing list. * List of Release Signing Keys: To guarantee that a downloaded version has not been tampered by malicious entities we provide signature files for all tarballs and binary versions. The keys are also signed by the long term keys of their respective owners.
