📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you're tired of a mass culture that pumps out Harry Potter reboot series and Chris Pratt films so bad even AI couldn't generate them, why not revisit one of the great films of the 20th Century. Ingmar Bergman's "Persona" is currently available to watch on HBO Max, and offers a wonderfully confounding, disturbing yet lyrical experience that any film fan should see at least once. You're not going to have much of a clue about what's going on, but that's sort of the point.

Industry observers note that the 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity. "Persona" was the realization of that vision. It stars Liv Ullmann as an actress named Elisabet who during a stage performance suddenly stops speaking and moving. Her doctor advises she be taken to a remote seaside cottage to be nursed back to health. That job falls to nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson) who in her frequent one-sided conversations with her mute patient reveals candid details of her own past. As their time together goes on, Alma and Elisabet begin to assume each other's identities.

Aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann. Andersson had worked with Bergman regularly since their first collaboration on "Smiles of a Summer Night" in 1955. "Persona" was, however, Norwegian actress Liv Ullmann's first Bergman film. Given the director's view of it as a "sonata" for the pair, it would seem the filmmaker was interested in his actors more than anything else.

But "Persona" is full of fascinating symbolism and is thematically rich enough that it's spawned endless critical analysis interpreting the film as everything from a modernist horror movie to an interrogation of acting itself as an art form. It's also been interpreted as an exploration of the distinction between our true selves and the masks we wear in social settings — which, considering the film's title, clearly has some relevance.

But even Roger Ebert admitted to not understanding the movie upon his initial viewing in 1967. When the critic revisited "Persona" in 2001, he still seemed somewhat perplexed, even while writing, "I know most of what I am ever likely to know about films, and I think I understand that the best approach to 'Persona' is a literal one." The ending of "Persona" certainly offers no answers, but it's not supposed to. Susan Sontag wrote that "Persona" is "bound to trouble, perplex and frustrate most filmgoers," and it does — but in the most beautiful, mesmeric, and disturbing way possible. The film is streaming on HBO Max at the time of writing, but can also be found on the usual digital platforms as well as on archive.org for free.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

In a recent development, on Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Industry observers note that colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • Sources indicate that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • Industry observers note that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Sources indicate that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

Industry observers note that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado stated. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

According to recent reports, for Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

It has been revealed that still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

Sources indicate that this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford noted, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

Latest Update: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • It has been revealed that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

It has been revealed that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering upcoming security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be stated for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

Sources indicate that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October revision. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Industry observers note that it's notable to understand that just about every firm that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as promptly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one manufacturer, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remake of the classic horror film, American Psycho, receives an unfortunate upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that luca Guadagnino's planned American Psycho remake has received a long-awaited but upsetting revision. The director has revealed that his new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' bestselling novel is no longer moving forward, bringing an end to years of uncertainty surrounding the project.

During an appearance on Deadline's Crew Call podcast with Anthony D'Alessandro, Guadagnino addressed the status of his American Psycho remake. Although he praised the screenplay written by Scott Z. Burns, the director revealed that the project is no longer happening. However, he did not explain why the film has been canceled or whether there are any prepares to revive it in the future.

It has been revealed that scott Z Burns wrote a fantastic script. Unfortunately for me, as we speak, it's not happening.

The project was first announced in October 2024. Lionsgate confirmed that it had been developing a remake of Ellis' 1991 novel, with Burns writing the screenplay and Guadagnino directing. However, instead of just recreating the 2000 Christian Bale-led movie, the upcoming adaptation was going to offer audiences a different take on the original story.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, shortly after the studio declared the project, it faced several obstacles, especially when it came to finding an actor to portray Patrick Bateman. Austin Butler was reportedly linked to the leading role in December 2024, but his involvement was never officially confirmed by Guadagnino.

In early 2025, Ellis explained that the movie had not secured the rights it needed to move forward. Despite the author's comments, Guadagnino was still optimistic about the film during CinemaCon in April 2025, discussing the screenplay's development and his love for the book.

Released in 2000, American Psycho is a psychological horror film directed by Mary Harron, who co-wrote the screenplay with Guinevere Turner. The movie stars Bale as Bateman, a successful Fresh York City investment banker who seems like a normal enough person but is actually a serial killer. The film also featured several other iconic actors, including Willem Dafoe, Jared Leto, Josh Lucas, Chloë Sevigny, Samantha Mathis, Justin Theroux, and Reese Witherspoon.

American Psycho's producer Edward R. Pressman acquired the adaptation rights in 1992, and several directors, such as David Cronenberg and Stuart Gordon, were interested in directing the project. Although Harron chose Bale for the leading role, the studio was also considering casting Leonardo DiCaprio.

American Psycho was based on a novel of the same name. The book was written from Bateman's perspective. Its graphic and intricate descriptions of violence and other disturbing content caused a lot of controversy, resulting in a ton of restrictions being placed on it when it comes to selling the book. However, the book was never outright banned in any country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 6 has a giant crab haunting the swamps and, more importantly, the Crabshack VF5 SMG, a crab-themed gun, to help your future career prospects. It's all part of an optional event called Pelican Valley Outpost that sees you pick up the pieces of some questionable experiments carried out on behalf of a store chain. It's worth the trouble, even aside from the standout weapon. There's some cash to help reach your next family fund milestone and a free jet ski, too. Best of all, this little excursion is completely safe, assuming you don't run afoul of the local gator population.

Below, we show you where to find the giant crab in GTA 6 so you can clear the Pelican Valley Outpost and get the Crabshack VF5 SMG.

In a recent development, pelican Valley Outpost, where the giant crab research facility is, has several codes you need to find on your way to getting the standout weapon. You'll find it on a medium-sized island southwest of the "Pelican Valley" name label on the map. Once you remove the fog from the region map, you can see it's one of the only islands in the area with buildings on it.

Industry observers note that take Jason's boat from his house, and set out. Definitely don't swim here, even if you're already nearby. There are too many gators for this to be a safe option. You can dock your boat at the boathouse and follow the jetty to the research facility proper. The boathouse is locked, but you'll get inside before leaving.

Sources indicate that you'll see several buildings in the compound, but if you venture inside the first shack, you'll notice the power is off. You can still explore it, though you can't access the researcher's computer, which is essential for clearing the outpost. Head outside and around the back of the building near the blue crab cages. Interact with the breaker box to turn the power on, and head back inside. Ignore the computer for now, and take a right. There's a bag of chips in the kitchen if you want Jason to pack on some calories, and the login password for the computer is in the small bedroom opposite the kitchen. Investigate the small piece of wood on the floor to see all the choices, with "CLEAVES" being the most recent.

Interact with the computer, and press left on the direction pad to enter CLEAVES. You can skim through a few tabs of information on-screen, but the important one is the note in the green cell that says "Safe code = Double Success." Leave when you're finished.

Sources indicate that karkinos, the giant crab from the report, will jump you in a short cutscene, but you don't have to fight her. Press the on-screen button to push her off, and she'll vanish into the swamp.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to get the giant crab safe code yourself, head to the research lab behind the shack next. There's a table with a trauma kit and some Zombix inside, which is handy, and in the specimen room you'll find Karkinos' former home and a list of experiments. Only one was a success, number 36. The code, "double success," refers to doubling the number of the successful experiment, making the code 0072.

Sources indicate that go back into the shack, and enter 0072 on the safe. Inside, you'll find a stack of money ($1,107 for us) and another note that reads "Emergency go protocol: 0212.".

The emergency protocol is the boathouse code. Leave the research compound, return to the boathouse, and input 0212 on the keypad. The door will open. Karkinos' caretaker wasn't as lucky as Jason, but their loss is your gain. Pick up the Crabshack VF5 SMG from their corpse, and you can grab a bag of marked bills to drop off at Brian's lockup later, too.

You can leave the compound the way you came, or you can hop on the jet ski and make your way home that way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Throughout its 60-year history, the "Star Trek" franchise has been the home to some truly fantastic voices.
  • Needless to say, those signature dulcet tones make him easy to pick out when you hear him showing up somewhere other than the bridge of the USS Enterprise, even when the character he's playing could not look any more different than the man himself.
  • It has been revealed that "Batman Beyond" debuted in 1999 when creators Bruce Timm, Paul Dini, and Alan Burnett came up with a desperate pitch to satisfy the studio's demand for a new Batman show: a slightly sci-fi, near-future take on the Dark Knight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Throughout its 60-year history, the "Star Trek" franchise has been the home to some truly fantastic voices. The dramatic, over-the-top delivery of William Shatner as Captain Kirk, the sonorous tones of Avery Brooks as Captain Sisko, and the cat-like vocal fry of Kate Mulgrew as Captain Janeway are, in their own way, as iconic as the ships they helmed. You don't need to go all the way to the captain's chair to find those voices, though. George Takei, who played Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu on the original "Trek," had a voice so recognizable that he was able to turn something as simple as "oh my" into a full-on catchphrase.

Needless to say, those signature dulcet tones make him easy to pick out when you hear him showing up somewhere other than the bridge of the USS Enterprise, even when the character he's playing could not look any more different than the man himself. So if you were catching up on one of the best Batman shows ever made, you were not having an audio hallucination. That was in fact George Takei as Mr. Fixx in the two-part pilot of "Batman Beyond.".

It has been revealed that "Batman Beyond" debuted in 1999 when creators Bruce Timm, Paul Dini, and Alan Burnett came up with a desperate pitch to satisfy the studio's demand for a new Batman show: a slightly sci-fi, near-future take on the Dark Knight. Set decades after the events of "Batman: The Animated Series," the series followed high school student Terry McGinnis (Will Friedle) as he took over the role of Batman from a retired Bruce Wayne, played by legendary "BTAS" voice actor Kevin Conroy. Terry's youth, struggles balancing his Batman identity with life as a cool teen, and wisecracking demeanor gave the character a vibe that was equal parts Batman and Spider-Man. That may have turned off a few viewers at the time who thought a teenage Batman was a ripoff, but the end result speaks for itself.

Industry observers note that while he only appeared in the first two episodes, Takei's character was arguably the most vital villain in the entire series. Derek Powers, who would go on to become the supervillain Blight, might've been the mastermind who ordered the hit, but it was Mr. Fixx who actually killed Terry's father and set him on the path of vengeance that would lead to him becoming Batman. The casting was an interesting one, too. Fixx had the design of a hulking brute with a scarred eye, but even a few words in Takei's rich voice gave him a depth that subverted looks and hinted at a much deeper character. Unfortunately, that character wound up at the bottom of the ocean off the coast of Gotham City before we could really get into his hopes and dreams, but that's the life of an evil henchman for you.

Takei wasn't the only notable celebrity on "Batman Beyond." Hardcore rocker Henry Rollins had a recurring role as D-list supervillain Mad Stan, former James Bond actor George Lazenby highlighted up as King, the leader of the Royal Flush Gang, and "Terminator" star Linda Hamilton made an appearance as a scientist who built a new body for a cryogenically preserved Mr. Freeze, among others. Cary Elwes, Tim Curry, Michael McKean, Ice-T ... the list goes on, and it's full of compelling performances that helped to make the show the beloved classic that it is.

It has been revealed that if you've got a good ear, "Batman Beyond" is worth watching just for spotting celebrity voices. And if you don't, well, it's worth watching because it's a great take on Batman with some phenomenal episodes and a great design sense. Just don't be surprised if you find yourself thinking some of those supervillains sound awfully familiar.

Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest fresh director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really swiftly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” mentioned Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-unveiled third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Fresh Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest fresh director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

Recent findings suggest that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really swiftly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” mentioned Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

Industry observers note that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” mentioned Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

It has been revealed that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” remarked Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how promptly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

Industry observers note that “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” remarked Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, rapidly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

It has been revealed that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” mentioned Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

Industry observers note that “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” remarked Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Industry observers note that the "Hunger Games" universe is full of wild, larger-than-life characters, especially when we're talking about denizens of the ultra-wealthy and super-powerful Capitol that controls Panem. Every year, during the annual Hunger Games that cull (or "reap") children from each of Panem's tightly controlled and impoverished 12 districts, Capitol citizens help beautify those kids before sending most of them to their deaths, and many Capitol higher-ups pursue plastic surgery and extreme fashion for high-concept looks.

One of those people in the latest "Hunger Games" book and movie, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is the erratic and unreliable District 12 stylist Magno Stift, who's legally married to the surgically-enhanced District 12 chaperone Drusilla Sickle (an unrecognizable Glenn Close in the film) and who's played on screen by Billy Porter. In the novel, our protagonist Haymitch Abernathy — a young version of the District 12 victor played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" films and Joseph Zada in this latest prequel — notes that nobody speaks highly of Magno, and "he's every bit as bad as they say." He continues, "While the other stylists do new costumes each year for the parade and interviews that happen before the Games, he seems to have a limitless supply of the same crappy coal miner overalls in an array of sizes.".

Sources indicate that when Magno finally demonstrates up, we see him through Haymitch's eyes: "Magno Stift's sun-leathered skin has been tattooed with a snakeskin pattern. He wears a long shirt made of metal diamonds and no visible pants. His sandals lace all the way up to his pelvis, and from each of his ears dangle tiny, living garter snakes that twist and turn in misery." Eventually, he stops showing up to work when one of his wearable reptiles poisons him. So, why does Magno look familiar in the movie?

According to recent reports, you've definitely seen Magno Stift actor Billy Porter in at least one of his recent high-profile projects, so let me walk you through some of them. After earning fame and acclaim for his role as Lola in the Broadway stage musical version of "Kinky Boots," which won him a Tony and a Grammy, Porter's massive-screen career slowly began to take off. Though he did, to be totally fair, appear as a singer in the 1996 classic "The First Wives Club," Porter's newfound name recognition in the 2010s earned him roles in films like "The Humbling" alongside Greta Gerwig and Al Pacino, the 2020 comedy "Like a Boss" with Tiffany Haddish, and 2021's "Cinderella," which gave Porter one of his biggest roles yet as the fairy godparent Fab G.

Recent findings suggest that during a 2021 interview with People Magazine, Porter talked about gender-flipping the role played by none other than Whitney Houston in the much-loved 1997 TV film adaptation of the stage musical "Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella" starring Brandy. "When I was 14, my dream was to be the male Whitney Houston," the actor quipped before adding, ""Magic has no gender. That is the most vital for me.".

After starring in "Cinderella" with Camilla Cabello and James Corden, Porter directed the coming-of-age film "Anything's Possible," popped up in the senior comedy "80 for Brady," and got dramatic in "Our Son" with Luke Evans and Andrew Rannells. So, what about Porter's small-screen career? It's booming, too.

Sources indicate that billy Porter's early years on TV include credits on "So You Think You Can Dance" as a performer and stalwart procedurals like "Law & Order," as well as its massively successful spin-off "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" — but after winning that Tony and Emmy and hosting an eight-episode 2013 special called "Land of Lola: Backstage at Kinky Boots," Porter was finally on the map. Aside from "American Horror Story: Apocalypse" and other recurring and guest arcs on demonstrates like the 2021 "Gossip Girl" reboot, Porter's most recognizable role is as Prayerful "Pray" Tell, an emcee in the New York ballroom scene, on Ryan Murphy's series "Pose." Not only did Porter get the chance to play a character who shares his HIV diagnosis (something the actor revealed in his own life in 2021), he won an Emmy for playing Pray Tell and became the first-ever gay Black man to win in any lead Emmy category. As Porter told People Magazine in 2021, it was also an important role for him for other reasons:.

In a recent development, "'Pose' and Pray Tell have been a proxy for my healing. The trauma was so difficult. The grief was so heavy. The antiretroviral drugs [for HIV] came, and everybody moved on. There's a whole generation of us that really never got a chance to process having lived through the AIDS crisis [and] having lived through an epidemic.".

You can see Billy Porter (briefly) play Magno Stift in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is currently playing in theaters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary.
  • Industry observers note that players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2.
  • Sources indicate that what's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary. This thing's a life sim. GTA 6's life sim bona fides are so undeniable that, within the first two days of its release, a not-insignificant swath of players have eschewed the elaborate robberies and high-tension shootouts to instead embrace the ancient gaming tradition of "finding IRL locations and Leo memeing at them.".

Industry observers note that players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2. But with GTA 6, which takes place in a satirized version of Florida called Leonida, players were always going to take it to another level. This game is from Rockstar Games, a studio so well-known for its attention to detail it once infamously implemented horse testicles that shrink in reaction to cold weather. GTA 6 has been in development for a decade. Its leads have conducted "research" trips to Miami-Dade County for just as long. A perfect storm for some ridiculously faithful world design that's resulted in brain-melting levels of realism.

Sources indicate that what's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those. It's also found in recreations of nondescript buildings you'd otherwise never think twice about. This design ethos is best illustrated in one viral clip in which an unidentified creator films Jason walking through an apartment complex before coming to a stop on a patio overlooking a South Beach meridian. The creator, continuing to film, stands up in real life, then walks out of their own front door and onto a patio of the same exact building. ("This is crazy [exploding head emoji]," they wrote. "My apartment is in a video game.").

Even in the realm of sports, Rockstar wasn't just drawn to the major leagues. Yes, GTA 6 includes a riff on Miami's Kaseya Cener (homebase of the Miami Heat), but it also includes a pixel-perfect facsimile of the Miami Marine Stadium. Built in the early '60s as a regatta venue, the stadium went on to host film shoots, presidential rallies, and concerts from the likes of Queen, The Who, Jimmy Buffet, and other megawatt stars, according to the nonprofit Restore Miami Marine Stadium. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew took the venue out of commission. It's spent the past three decades collecting rust and graffiti. But in GTA 6, it's just...there. (In August of this year, Miami voters passed a referendum that paves the way for a potential restoration.).

Industry observers note that fans have been unpacking these references throughout the entirety of GTA 6's marketing cycle. Following Rockstar's release of the second GTA 6 trailer, back in May 2025, I could've sworn — based on a vanishingly brief 0.5-second glance — that the South Beach party spot The Clevelander would serve as a location in the game. The bar's marketing department never responded to my initial request for comment. Now that I've played, I can confirm that, yes, it's absolutely in the game, in all its flamingo-pink glory. The Clevelander is somewhat of an institution, having remained a South Beach party spot for decades on the back of some extremely lucky local ordinances, but at face value, it's not all that distinct from any other South Beach bar: neon lights, a questionable pool, overpriced drinks. And yet, it's in GTA 6 too.

It has been revealed that the locations GTA 6 players seem drawn to point out tend to be in the Miami metropolitan area, which makes sense: It's the population nexus of the state. But Vice City encompasses a small portion of Leonida's map, and Florida itself poses no shortage of things to reference beyond the Miami-Dade County limits. Who knows what players will find and Leo meme at? Though there's one thing not worth seeking out. In its quest to construct an alternate reality, Rockstar neglected to include arguably the most Florida landmark of them: Disney World.

5 Best Hercule Poirot Movies, Ranked Worst To Best

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that agatha Christie is one of the most popular authors of all time.
  • Recent findings suggest that then there’s Hercule Poirot, arguably Christie’s most popular fictional character.
  • According to recent reports, it’s no surprise, then, that Hercule Poirot was brought to movie theaters soon after.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that agatha Christie is one of the most popular authors of all time. The English writer crafted many classic stories in the 20th century, and introduced a number of iconic heroes, many of whom are still being adapted to this day. One of these characters is Miss Marple, who made her debut in 1927, when she featured in a short story titled The Tuesday Night Club, which was published in The Royal Magazine.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s Hercule Poirot, arguably Christie’s most popular fictional character. Christie first introduced the Belgian detective in The Mysterious Affair at Styles, which was written in 1916 and published four years later in 1920. Poirot was a popular character upon release, but Christie’s hero became a sensation around six years later.

According to recent reports, it’s no surprise, then, that Hercule Poirot was brought to movie theaters soon after. The character made his massive screen debut in 1931s Alibi, with Austin Trevor playing the hero. However, Trevor’s iteration of Poirot deviated greatly from Christie’s books in many ways, including not sporting the detective’s classic mustache.

Since then, dozens of actors have gone on to play Poirot in both movies and television. Arguably the greatest Poirot adaptation of all is David Suchet’s series, which began in 1989, but the detective has still had plenty of excellent films, too. For example, both Peter Ustinov and, more recently, Kenneth Branagh helmed Poirot mystery movies that were received with great acclaim.

The most famous Poirot story, in both literature and film and television, is Murder on the Orient Express. Christie first crafted this story in the early 1930s, and it was initially published as a six-part series in the Saturday Evening Post under the name Murder on the Calais Coach. With Murder on the Orient Express, Christie created the perfect locked-in mystery, with all the characters stuck on a train for days, knowing that one (or more) of them is a murderer.

Recent findings suggest that kenneth Branagh took on the role of Poirot, and the responsibility of adapting Christie’s iconic work, in 2017s Murder on the Orient Express remake. Like many Poirot movies that were released in the 20th century, Branagh assembled an exciting group of actors to play the train occupants. The cast included Johnny Depp, Michelle Pfeiffer, Judi Dench, Penélope Cruz, Willem Dafoe, Daisy Ridley, Leslie Odom Jr., Josh Gad, Derek Jacobi, Olivia Colman, and Tom Bateman.

Branagh’s remake was successful in many ways. The cast was exceptional, especially Michelle Pfeiffer and Willem Dafoe. Additionally, the film looked spectacular, with a blue and white color palette radiating from the screen. Branagh is a critically acclaimed director, and he certainly brought his A-game to this movie.

According to recent reports, yet, Murder on the Orient Express (2017) struggled in some areas, too. For many, the film felt overly familiar, which may be a harsh criticism given that the story is nearly one hundred years old and has been told dozens of times (and in many different languages, too). Additionally, Branagh’s portrayal of Poirot was a bit of a mixed bag. He captured the essence of the character well, but was vastly different physically from how Poirot is described in the books.

The best of Kenneth Branagh’s three Poirot films was his last, A Haunting in Venice. With this film, it felt as if Branagh had finally found his voice in telling a Hercule Poirot story, both as a director and as an actor. Branagh seems at his most comfortable on screen in this film, and works well within the darker tone that A Haunting in Venice provides.

At the same time, this film felt less predictable than the two that came before, in part because it wasn’t adapting one of Christie’s most famous novels (and because it took more liberties from its source material, too).

In a recent development, peter Ustinov played Poirot in six films in total, three of which were released in theaters, with the others going straight to television. One of the theatrical releases was Death on the Nile (1978), a film that serves as a much better adaptation of the story than Branagh’s. Like most of the other Poirot films, this movie recruited several high-profile actors.

There was Peter Ustinov as Hercule Poirot, and he was joined by David Niven, Lois Chiles, Simon MacCorkindale, Mia Farrow, Bette Davis, Maggie Smith, Angela Lansbury, Olivia Hussey, George Kennedy, and Jack Warden. Of these, Mia Farrow, Maggie Smith, and Angela Lansbury truly stood out, all giving exceptional performances. The surrounding film was excellent, too, with amazing visuals (having actually been filmed on location) and a captivating script adaptation of Christie’s original story.

Another Ustinov Poirot film is Evil Under the Sun, which was released in 1982. This is Ustinov’s best Poirot movie, in part because the English actor finds his groove to the fullest here. He’s charming, witty, and genuinely funny, too (such as in the scene where Poirot pretends to swim in a bathing suit).

Industry observers note that like Death on the Nile (1978), Evil Under the Sun also has jaw-dropping visuals, having once again been filmed on location. The film itself is more playful than its predecessors, too, which makes it more entertaining overall.

Sources indicate that four decades after the story was first released, Murder on the Orient Express made its way to the substantial screen with a film of the same name. This movie is a relatively faithful adaptation of the book, telling the story of the murder of American businessman Samuel Ratchett (aka Richard Widmark) aboard the famous Orient Express. From there, Poirot is forced to investigate the crime, and prevent the train journey from getting any more deadly.

Murder on the Orient Express (1974) had a star-studded cast. Albert Finney played Poirot, and did so with his usual charm and enthusiasm. Finney was joined by a number of A-list actors, too, including Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman, Sean Connery, John Gielgud, Vanessa Redgrave, Michael York, Anthony Perkins, and Martin Balsam. Upon the release of the film, the ensemble cast was praised for their respective performances.

In fact, several of these performers received accolades for their work in the film. For example, Bergman won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Greta Ohlsson. More broadly, the film itself was the recipient of six Oscar nominations in total, and that includes a Best Actor nomination for Finney and Best Adapted Screenplay for writer Paul Dehn.

According to recent reports, the praise that this adaptation received was well deserved, too. The film does a spectacular job of bringing Christie’s story to the significant screen, making these characters (and Hercule Poirot in particular) truly come alive. This film may be a bit dated when watching it in the modern day, however, but Christie’s story still remains timeless in many ways.

#86016. The Downfall Of The Terminator Franchise Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (887 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

The Downfall Of The Terminator Franchise Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films?
  • The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold.
  • It has been revealed that it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films? Setting aside the usual caveat that no sequel can hope to match the dizzying heights of some of the most influential sci-fi/action/horror movies of all time, it's a decent question. After all, every "Terminator" movie save one has involved star Arnold Schwarzenegger in a key role, so it's not like his absence has hurt the series. And even though the return of another key actor in the series, Linda Hamilton, helped 2019's "Terminator: Dark Fate," that film still had its problems. A conventional wisdom answer to the problem of rescuing the "Terminator" series is that the original creator/director James Cameron should fully come back and make another installment, yet his involvement with "Dark Fate" means success wouldn't necessarily be guaranteed.

The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold. One issue is the staggering example set by the first two films, which would be hard for any franchise to overcome. The other concerns the one moment that the downfall of the franchise can be traced back to, which is ironically one of the moments most cited by fans as a highlight of the series: the ending of 2003's "Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines." To be fair, most of "Terminator 3," despite its decent quality, is to blame for putting the franchise on a path it can't quite escape from. Yet it's the ending, as bold as it is, which struck a deterministic note that ended up being too harsh for the series to bear. "Terminator" has always been dark, yet its hopeful subtext is key to its recipe, and that's something which has been left out of every installment since "Terminator 2.".

It has been revealed that it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one. After all, these are movies in which Linda Hamilton's Sarah Connor is on the run for her life from an unstoppable killing machine, where either she or her young son John suddenly find themselves having to survive the threats of a dark future while having little help from the modern day around them. Yet an crucial thing to remember about "The Terminator" is that Skynet's initiative to assassinate Sarah by sending a Terminator back in time was only implemented because John wins the war against the machines in the future. "The Terminator" is a time travel story, and is thus subject to the various paradoxes inherent to the genre. Yet its tale has a deterministic logic to it, one which is predicated on humans surviving despite their near-annihilation by the machines.

"Terminator 3" effectively undoes the ambiguous hopeful ending of "Terminator 2," where Sarah and John had possibly prevented Judgment Day for good. While the third film's logic is sound from a time travel point of view (i.e. how could any "Terminator" movie have happened if Judgement Day never does), it does make "Terminator 2" feel too much like it was all for nought. Adding to that quiet despair is the bigger tragedy of actually seeing Judgment Day occur, meaning that the efforts of a now adult John (Nick Stahl) to try and stop it from happening again make not just "Terminator 2" but most of "Terminator 3" feel deflating. The ending of "Terminator 3" is a great example of how a cool twist can work logically, yet emotionally undermine a film (and, in this case, a franchise) too much.

Sources indicate that the first two "Terminator" films leaned into the time travel paradox by presenting a deterministic situation while supporting free will. "There's no fate but what we make for ourselves" is a key phrase which can be interpreted several ways, as either a bitter observation or a message of hope. While the deterministic path that "Terminator 3" and "Terminator Salvation" took was logically sound, they didn't provide enough of the aspirational side; the latter film was a time travel story in subtext only.

Industry observers note that the next two movies in the franchise course-corrected in a bizarre way, embracing the wide-open possibilities of the series' time travel component with little to no regard for the characters or the audience. "Genisys" is too pleased with its twists to let any of them land emotionally. In comparison, "Dark Fate" has much richer characterizations, yet it alienates from the opening twist, and turns the series' lore on its head in a way that doesn't fully land. The franchise's one shining moment post-"Terminator 2," the TV series "Terminator: The Sarah Connor Chronicles," was sadly canceled just as the intricate narrative it weaved was bearing the type of lore-changing fruit that "Genisys" and "Dark Fate" tried too hard to grow.

In general, the "Terminator" sequels after "Judgment Day" have attempted to serve both the series' deterministic and free will concepts, which are inherently paradoxical. So, while every one of the "Terminator" sequels have introduced some fascinating (and occasionally excellent) ideas, they all revolve around an inescapable fate, whether it's one that already happened or one that will happen. While I believe the series' fate could still be changed, it's ironic that the thing we're hoping gets saved is now the "Terminator" films themselves.

Bolt's Scooters Are Becoming Accessibility Sensors

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geoawesome

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle.
  • During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the company used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility.
  • Bolt claims the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle. It can also be a mobile geospatial sensor.

During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the company used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility.

Bolt claims the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments. The resulting information was contributed to OpenStreetMap, according to Bolt’s accessibility programme page.

Sources indicate that publishing the results as open data makes the project more significant than a conventional corporate mapping exercise. Municipalities, routing applications and accessibility services could all potentially use the observations.

It has been revealed that the larger opportunity is the conversion of commercial vehicle fleets into continuously operating urban-observation networks. Thousands of scooters already traverse city streets during everyday operations, potentially detecting damaged surfaces and deteriorating infrastructure without requiring a dedicated municipal survey.

It has been revealed that according to Geo Week News, Bolt combined GPS with accelerometers, gyroscopes and cameras. The organization reports that the pilot increased available surface-quality data in Tallinn by 26%. These figures have not been independently audited.

According to recent reports, the difficult step is converting motion signals into reliable accessibility information. A vibration could represent broken pavement, cobblestones, a drainage channel or an abrupt rider manoeuvre. Results may also vary with speed, tyre pressure, weather and scooter model.

Coverage presents another limitation. Scooters primarily travel where their use is permitted and commercially viable. They may miss residential streets, pedestrian paths and disconnected sections that create the greatest problems for wheelchair owners.

Each observation therefore needs provenance, a confidence level and an effective validation method. The most vital validators should include wheelchair and mobility-aid owners, who can determine whether a detected anomaly represents a genuine barrier.

Wheels4Wheels complements rather than replaces existing accessibility platforms. Wheelmap maps the accessibility of public places, while Project Sidewalk combines crowdsourcing, machine learning and street imagery to identify curb ramps and obstacles. Bolt adds passive, recurring fleet sensing.

A future workflow could use scooter telemetry to flag anomalies, imagery to classify them and local contributors to confirm their significance before the information enters OpenStreetMap.

Public discussion of the project has also highlighted a contradiction: poorly parked scooters can themselves block sidewalks and curb ramps. Bolt’s accessibility strategy must therefore address parking and obstruction management alongside data collection.

Recent findings suggest that if the company can demonstrate reliable classification, transparent data handling and meaningful participation by accessibility users, Wheels4Wheels could evolve into more than a mapping experiment. The sensing capacity already exists. The next challenge is turning it into trustworthy, routable and genuinely inclusive geospatial infrastructure.

Industry observers note that for decades, “more bands” in Earth observation meant one of two things: you either work with multispectral sensors; four to ten broad bands, cheap, fast and familiar or else transition to the hyperspectral domain, which has hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands, costly and enormous data volumes. However, this gap is closing not by making hyperspectral high-resolution accessible, but by rethinking what “enough bands” actually means. A category is quietly establishing itself between the two: Superspectral, a curated set of roughly a dozen to a few dozen discrete bands, placed purposely at specific wavelengths that correspond to something physically meaningful, rather than being sampled continuously across the electromagnetic spectrum.

In a recent development, multispectral sensors were built around a simple idea: a handful of broad bands such as blue, green, red, red-edge, near-infrared are enough to compute NDVI & NDRE, delineate landcover, and monitor vegetation vigour at scale. Many of these systems also carry a panchromatic band: a single high-resolution spectral channel spanning across the visible spectrum (400-800 nm), used purely to sharpen spatial detail rather than to add spectral information. That’s the multispectral-era trade-off at minimal where spatial resolution and spectral resolution were treated as two separate problems, solved by two different types of bands. It works and it still works, for a huge share of remote sensing applications.

However, broad bands average out the very features that distinguish stressed vegetation from healthy vegetation, one water body from another, or one mineral from the next. A 100-120 nm wide band cannot resolve a narrow absorption or reflectance feature within it. Indices tied to specific physiological or physical processes such as pigment ratios, early-stage stress signatures and water turbidity, often require reflectance captured at precise, narrow wavelengths which a standard four or five-band setup was never designed to capture.

Why Hyperspectral isn’t the Universal Answer.

Hyperspectral imaging solves the problem by capturing contiguous and narrow bands. A 20-band sensor covering 500-700 nm at 10 nm interval is hyperspectral by this definition, while a sensor with 20 discrete, non-adjacent bands spanning the visible through infrared is still, technically a multispectral. That distinction matters because hyperspectral sensors carry real expense; complex optics, strict calibration requirements, and data volumes that stretch onboard storage, downlink bandwidth, and downstream ML pipelines. For most applied problems, that’s more data than the underlying problem statement actually needs.

The Middle Category: Superspectral.

Sources indicate that superspectral fits between the two. Rather than sampling the electromagnetic spectrum continuously, it samples it selectively – a dozen-plus discrete, narrow bands chosen because they align with known absorption or reflectance features, not because they happen to be adjacent on a continuum. It’s a knowledge-first approach to sensor design: instead of asking “how much of the spectrum can we cover continuously,” it asks “which specific wavelengths actually carry the signal we care about.”.

This only works if the band selection is grounded in the underlying physics or biology of the target. Which is exactly where the reasoning gets interesting — because the “right” dozen bands look completely different depending on what you’re trying to measure.

Building the Case: Three Domains, Three Different Superspectral Stacks.

According to recent reports, water quickly absorbs longer wavelengths, which is exactly why coastal and bathymetric applications require the shorter wavelength of the visible spectrum. In clear, deep water 400-450 nm wavelength penetrates furthest, making it the band of choice for shallow-water bathymetry and seafloor mapping. In turbid or CDOM-rich coastal water the picture inverts: suspended sediment and dissolved organic matter absorb and scatter strongly in the blue, and the transmission peak migrates toward green. On sediment loaded reef sites it has been observed shifting by around 100 nm into the green-yellow, peaking near 575 nm. A standard multispectral blue band, which is broadly tuned for atmospheric correction and land applications, is not optimized for this; a narrow, purpose-placed coastal-blue bands are. This is a case where one extra, carefully positioned band is more beneficial for the application than several additional generic ones.

Recent findings suggest that extending the vegetation logic straight into urban environments using Red-edge and NIR bands, but the physics doesn’t transfer as cleanly. Red-edge and NIR bands are diagnostic of chlorophyll and canopy structure, which makes them excellent for mapping urban vegetation fraction: street trees, park canopy, green-roof coverage, and green-space stress, all of which are legitimate and useful urban indicators, especially as proxies for urban surface extent and heat island risk. But Red-edge and NIR bands are not, a strong basis for classifying built materials themselves — asphalt, concrete, and rooftops don’t have a red-edge-style feature the way vegetation does. The spectral region that most cleanly separates impervious surfaces from vegetation and bare soil sits further out, in the shortwave infrared, where built materials and natural surfaces diverge most sharply. A Red-edge/NIR-only superspectral stack can tell you a great deal about a city’s green infrastructure; it can’t, tell you what the non-green parts of the city are made of. Getting that requires extending the band selection into SWIR — which is a fair, extension of the same superspectral principle: add exactly the band the physics calls for, nothing more.

Superspectral Sensors Exists: Drones to Satellites.

In a recent development, micasense Drone payload: RedEdge-P Triple. A stacked triple narrowband camera bodies on one drone platform, each contributing a handful of 15 discrete, narrow, non-contiguous bands, pan-sharpened to 4 centimetres per pixel, enough to compute pigment and stress-sensitive indices that a standard five-band multispectral sensor can’t generate. This is the smallest-scale, most accessible end of the superspectral sensor; no continuous spectral coverage, just a deliberately chosen set of narrow bands.

Commercial VHR satellite: WorldView-3. Launched in 2014, WorldView-3 is explicitly described in the remote sensing literature and by its operators as a “Superspectral” sensor, a term used specifically to distinguish it from hyperspectral. Its imager collects 8 discrete VNIR bands (coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red-edge, and two NIR bands), 8 discrete SWIR bands, and a separate 12-band CAVIS instrument for atmospheric correction (clouds, aerosols, water vapor, ice, and snow) 29 bands in total, but none of them contiguous in the way a hyperspectral band are. That distinction matters: WorldView-3 has been used for tasks like hydrocarbon and mineral detection that’s the domain of hyperspectral, precisely because its SWIR bands were placed at known diagnostic absorption features rather than spread evenly across the spectrum.

According to recent reports, research microsatellite: VENμS. A joint French–Israeli mission (CNES and the Israel Space Agency, rolled out 2017), was purpose-built VENμS Super-Spectral Camera (VSSC) with exactly 12 narrow bands between 415–910 nm, at 5.3 m resolution with a 2-day revisit. The band placement was designed specifically around vegetation status and the chlorophyll red-edge, plus atmospheric correction. It’s one of the cleanest real-world matches to the “12-18 narrow, targeted bands” definition of superspectral, since it was purpose-built as a science mission rather than adapted from a broader commercial sensor.

Next-generation Landsat constellation: Landsat Next. Planned for launch in late 2030/early 2031, the USGS and NASA’s Landsat Next mission is explicitly presented as “26-band Superspectral”, more than double the 11 bands on Landsat 8 and 9. It combines refined versions of Landsat’s legacy bands, ten new bands targeting applications like harmful algal blooms and snow hydrology, and five thermal infrared bands. When, a government agency formally classifies its flagship imaging mission as “superspectral” rather than multispectral or hyperspectral, that’s a strong indication the category has moved from marketing language to an accepted technical classification.

Why This Matters for GeoAI Pipelines.

The pattern across all three domains is the same, and it’s the real reason for superspectral as a category:.

It has been revealed that the multispectral or hyperspectral is a simple binary choice. Superspectral won’t replace either, broadband multispectral remains the workhorse for large-scale, low-cost monitoring, and hyperspectral remains necessary where continuous spectral coverage matters, like detailed mineral mapping or ore detection. But for the growing set of problems that need specific physical or biological signals – water quality, vegetation stress, urban green infrastructure and many more; without the overhead of a full hyperspectral sensor system, superspectral is becoming the realistic answer. It’s less “how much of the spectrum can we see” and more “how much do we actually need to see, and where.”.

Superspectral systems, by design, only see what they were told to look for. That’s a real trade-off, not a compromise to gloss over, it’s the whole point of this technology.

How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’
