💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • According to recent reports, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

According to recent reports, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

It has been revealed that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he stated. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

How’s his French? “Zero,” he stated. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

Recent findings suggest that the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” noted Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” noted Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

It has been revealed that one serious problem for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he mentioned. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Sources indicate that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he noted. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Sources indicate that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he noted, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what a difference seven-odd months make. Near the tail-end of September 2011, Fox Searchlight dumped Kenneth Lonergan's "Margaret" six years after it was filmed, only for its star, Mark Ruffalo, to Hulk-out in "The Avengers" the following May. But even so, Lonergan's movie — one of the best of the 21st Century — deserves so much better than to merely be remembered as a box office bomb.

Sources indicate that you see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue. In my lifetime, I've seen Philip Seymour Hoffman and John C. Reilly make a meal out of Sam Shepard's "True West," Rosemary Harris and Elaine Stritch tear up Edward Albee's "A Delicate Balance," and Jeffrey Wright and Don Cheadle set the stage ablaze with Suzan-Lori Parks' "Topdog/Underdog." On that same level, a late-20-something Ruffalo caused an off-Broadway stir in the fall of 1996 with his portrayal of troubled teenager Walter Straub in Lonergan's finely wrought drama "This Is Our Youth." He exuded shaggily handsome charm as a purposeless kid with a short-term game strategy that involves absconding with $15,000 of his wealthy dirtbag father's money.

Lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a New York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. This is as close to a clean logline as you can get with Lonergan's rich, sophisticated text, which baffled its dilettante, bigoted, multi-millionaire producer Gary Gilbert.

Recent findings suggest that "Margaret" was a talent magnet. Kenneth Lonergan's blisteringly brilliant screenplay drew in Mark Ruffalo, Paquin, Matt Damon, J. Smith Cameron, Allison Janney, Matthew Broderick, Jean Reno, and Rosemarie DeWitt. The great Jeannie Berlin, a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nominee for her knockout work in 1972's "The Heartbreak Kid," also appeared in the movie (her first since 1990's "In the Spirit"), and she was dubbed Best Supporting Actress by the Village Voice Film Poll for her turn as the sister of the victim killed in the aforementioned accident.

"Margaret" is a drama without villains. Anna Paquin's Lisa is a misguided and impulsive teenager. She is in search of justice where nothing of the sort can be found and tracks down Ruffalo's bus driver. He's well aware of the threat she poses to his steady bus-driving job, though, and shoos her away. But she persists, and her version of the events of that deadly day aren't entirely wrong, yet she still shares some responsibility. Yet, she can't accept that, so her catharsis will not arrive via a conviction.

Structurally, "Margaret" splits its time between Lisa's errant pursuit of justice and her mother (Cameron) as she tries to connect with a suave suitor played by Reno. Everyone loses. But this loss forges a stronger bond between mother and daughter. It binds them anew during a Lincoln Center performance of "The Tales of Hoffman," where, wordlessly, they patch up their wounds. (Heal? No. Those scabs will always be pickable.).

Industry observers note that it would be nice if a movie like that could go toe-to-toe with something on the level of "The Avengers," but there it is. Still, if you only really know Lonergan for his Oscar-winning "Manchester by the Sea," make it a priority to finally watch "Margaret.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Star Wars: The Mandalorian & Grogu struggling at the box office, it seems Disney is continuing development on two upcoming Star Wars films. This summer, Star Wars: New Jedi Order and Dave Filoni’s untitled movie as in-development projects were confirmed to be in the works in industry publication Production Weekly, suggesting that despite delays and silence around the projects, they haven't been shelved.

It has been revealed that star Wars: Fresh Jedi Order will reportedly bring back Daisy Ridley as Rey (Skywalker) roughly 15 years after the events of Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker as she rebuilds the Jedi. Considering that the Star Wars fandom has largely negative feelings about the sequel trilogy, especially after The Rise of Skywalker, New Jedi Order’s direct ties to that film will pose a steep challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the project has cycled through several writers. Damon Lindelof (Lost, The Leftovers, Watchmen) and Justin Britt-Gibson were the original screenwriters before Disney fired them — the pair are currently working together on HBO’s superhero detective series, Lanterns. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight was also set to write, but left the project in 2024. Last January, Variety reported that George Nolfi (The Bourne Ultimatum) is now writing the script. Filmmaker Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is set to direct the film. Newly introduced Jedi Order was originally scheduled for release on Dec. 17, 2027, but was removed from Disney’s schedule in May 2025.

Details about Dave Filoni’s untitled film have been scarce, but Production Weekly includes the following description: “The story will focus on the New Republic and will conclude the interconnected narratives told in The Mandalorian, The Book of Boba Fett, Ahsoka, and other Disney Plus series.” While it was previously rumored that the film would tie into recent Disney Plus TV series, it will be interesting to see whether it maintains that premise after The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed at the box office.

This past January, Filoni took over as president and chief creative officer at Lucasfilm. Filoni has overseen numerous Star Wars TV series, including The Clone Wars, Rebels, Ahsoka, Maul – Shadow Lord, and more. While most of his series have been well received, he’s been criticized for requiring viewers to be familiar with an increasingly complicated and insular TV universe.

Sources indicate that the only Star Wars film with a concrete release date is Star Wars: Starfighter, which takes place five years after the events of Rise of Skywalker and stars Ryan Gosling as a pilot. Shawn Levy (Deadpool & Wolverine) is directing the movie. It will be released in theaters on May 28, 2027. While there haven't been many Star Wars films in recent years, the series has stayed active through great TV series like The Ninth Jedi and the recent Star Wars: Zero Tech giant tactics game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, laura Hurley has been writing about the entertainment industry for more than twelve years, after a decade as a content producer and editor at CinemaBlend after writing for WhatCulture and Examiner. Attending events like SCAD TVfest and San Diego Comic-Con over the course of her career, she has been immersed in the world of network, streaming, and cable TV.

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit generated more hype than usual ahead of season 28 thanks to a major milestone: the 600th episode. The long-running drama brought Christopher Meloni back to reprise his role as Elliot Stabler for the first time since Law & Order: Organized Crime was canceled, and longtime fans could look forward to the highly anticipated reunion between Stabler and Mariska Hargitay's Olivia Benson. Unfortunately, their reunion was unsatisfying. The 600th episode rewrote elements of their past. Now, as season 28 continues, another reunion could prove to be much more meaningful.

Several reunions from Benson's earliest days with Special Victims will, sadly, be impossible. SVU handled Richard Belzer's real-life passing by giving Munch a moving tribute. Then, the show killed off Dann Florek's Don Cragen in season 27 (though Florek is still displeased about Cragen's death). After the 600th episode, it seems Stabler won't be back for a long time, if at all. Fortunately, SVU is bringing back somebody else from the old days to work with Benson again.

Alexandra Cabot, the first full-time assistant district attorney for Manhattan's Special Victims Unit, will return in an upcoming season 28 episode. While details about actress Stephanie March's return as Cabot are scarce, the confirmation that Mariska Hargitay will work with another veteran of SVU's golden years provides something to look forward to. There's no indication she'll appear in SVU's upcoming fall finale. It's safe to assume NBC will heavily promote Alex Cabot's return to Law & Order: Special Victims Unit when it arrives in the latest year.

In a recent development, even though Cabot wasn't Benson's longest-running ADA during her 28 years (and counting) in the Special Victims Unit, the two formed such a strong bond that many consider Cabot one of Benson's top love interests. They never canonically coupled up, so they can't claim a spot on any official ranking of Olivia Benson's love interests, but their relationship makes Cabot the perfect person to bring back in such a milestone season.

Plenty of time has passed to build anticipation for a reunion between Benson and Cabot. Nine seasons have gone by since Stephanie March last appeared as a guest star on SVU, so there's a lot to catch up on. Though fans can always revisit her years as part of the cast on Peacock, Cabot's departure left lingering questions, even now, nearly a decade after her last appearance on the show.

Industry observers note that the stakes are also lower for their reunion than they were for Christopher Meloni's arrival as Stabler. Viewers are less likely to be unsatisfied with her return, no matter how it happens. If anything, a reunion with an old, less fraught friend could be just what Benson needs to realize that she should focus on her personal life instead of dedicating herself wholly to her job.

Benson's relationship with Stabler has been messy since season 1 in 1999; her relationship with Cabot was much healthier despite their occasional differences, and it's due for a revisit in 2028. The franchise hasn't spent years building up expectations for their relationship, not the way it did with Stabler. The first story to feature Stephanie March since season 19 could be exactly what season 28 needs to shake off the challenges with the 600th episode.

When the news broke that Christopher Meloni was returning for the 600th episode, the odds seemed good that the installment would celebrate Law & Order: SVU's origins much more effectively than the 500th episode did. Whether viewers were rooting for a romance or just wanted to see the old partners investigating a case again, Stabler's return could have been perfect for Benson's 600th episode. Instead, the episode rewrote some of their foundational history.

The issues that made Stabler such a questionable cop by the end of his time in the franchise didn't cause problems at first, and their partnership was more solid than it was dysfunctional. The 600th episode presented his behavior as more problematic from the start than season 1 ever did, all to motivate Benson to reevaluate herself. Plus, the episode's ending felt much more like a goodbye to Stabler (and Meloni) than a fitting acknowledgment of a historic 600-episode run.

It has been revealed that as much as Meloni deserved a better exit than the abrupt cancellation of Law & Order: Organized Crime, his massive exit shouldn't have come at the expense of Benson's character in such a huge milestone. After all, Stabler hadn't been a series regular on SVU since 2011. It didn't help that the episode opened by revealing the two old partners hadn't spoken in a year and a half. Stabler even denied they were friends.

Recent findings suggest that if it had been a setup for them to resolve their challenges later in the season, the twist wouldn't have been a problem. As Stabler's final appearance in season 28 (and possibly his final appearance ever on SVU), it just wasn't satisfying. Reuniting with Cabot likely won't end in tears for Benson, and the two women will hopefully capitalize on their chemistry in their season 28 episode.

Industry observers note that stephanie March's episode of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit will be the ninth episode of the season. The fall finale will be the seventh, so Cabot will be back on our screens early in the new year.

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit season 28's fall finale airs Thursday, December 3, at 9 PM ET on NBC.

Industry observers note that even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a upcoming popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

In a recent development, but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

According to recent reports, “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he noted. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

Star Trek: The Motion Picture Was The First Movie To Feature This Iconic Marketing Tie-In

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that since the starship Enterprise first released its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world.
  • There is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in.
  • Recent findings suggest that long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that since the starship Enterprise first released its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world. Astronaut Mae Jemison, for example, credited Nichelle Nichols' performance as Lt. Uhura with inspiring her to become the first African-American woman to make it into space. Even the flip phones of the '90s were at least partially inspired by the design of the communicators on the original "Trek.".

There is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in. That's right: "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was the first movie to be featured in a Happy Meal.

Recent findings suggest that long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families. McDonald's executives liked the idea and hired advertiser Bob Bernstein, who decided to bundle those smaller portions into a box that would feature bright, kid-friendly colors and a small toy to keep the youngsters entertained while mom and dad threw down on their Significant Macs. Thus, the Happy Meal was born, and after being tested in 1977, it rolled out nationwide in 1979.

Needless to say, it was a hit with customers, but the last piece of this familiar fry-scented puzzle would come at the end of the year, when "Star Trek" was revived for the big screen with the entire main cast of the show returning to their roles. When the film ran over budget during production — not to mention injuries and other problems plaguing the set — Paramount's Vice President of Marketing and Licensing, Dawn Steel, was tasked with figuring out how to cover some of the rapidly expanding costs. She went looking for brand partners, and apparently someone at McDonald's was enough of a Trekkie to go for it. This approach was so successful that it would become almost mandatory for blockbuster movies to have some sort of fast-food tie-in as the years went on, a marketing tactic that would even change the direction of entire franchises, like it did with the infamous "Batman Returns" tie-in.

Recent findings suggest that looking back, doing a Happy Meal tie-in for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was, well, kind of a weird choice. As much as "Trek" had become a cultural touchstone due to the popularity of syndicated re-runs after its original three-season run, the film is a pretty slow, ponderous affair. It's largely about negotiating with a sentient space cloud, punctuated with bits of action like the scene where two members of the ship's crew die screaming for almost a full minute in a transporter accident. It's not a particularly gory or violent movie and there's nothing too objectionable, but it's not exactly "Bambi" — which would get its own Happy Meal tie-in in 1988 — either.

It's especially funny to think about the movie's slow-paced meditations on the unknown and the toll of aging in the context of the Happy Meal itself. Considering that the ad for the Happy Meal involved a Klingon yelling things like "yum-yum" and laughing at the jokes printed on the boxes, they might have given kids a bit of an unrealistic idea of what they were going to get at the movie theater.

  • Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo customers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most people, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

In a recent development, on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great fresh option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces fresh iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a newly introduced setting so owners can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

Sources indicate that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It has been revealed that it’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo consumers will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

I've been testing the Kayano for many years and while there have been some changes made with the Asics Gel-Kayano 33, I rate the Gel-Kayano 32 the better buy thanks to this deal.

Recent findings suggest that I keep hoping to see the Novablast 5 drop cheaper than this in the sales, but so far it's stuck firmly at $129, which is no doubt a sign of its popularity. I rate the Novablast as the best Asics cushioned shoe myself, because it's lighter and livelier than the Nimbus and Cumulus. While the Asics Novablast 6 is an excellent update the Novablast 5 remains a great daily trainer worth considering at this lower price.

Industry observers note that I'm currently testing the Asics Gel-Nimbus 29, which has a very different feel to the 28 thanks to a softer midsole foam. Many will prefer the upcoming shoe for this, but it actually strays into the 'too soft' category for me, sapping the energy at times during runs. If you don't want to take that risk, the Gel-Nimbus 28 is a reliable cushioned cruiser that's reduced by $40 in the sales.

Recent findings suggest that the Asics Superblast 3 is one of the better running shoes I've tested this year, but I'd still eye up this deal on the Superblast 2 in the sales if you're looking for a versatile max-cushioned sneaker. It's great for all kinds of runs, and I often used the Superblast 2 for trips with a lot of walking as well.

According to recent reports, nick Harris-Fry is an experienced health and fitness journalist, writing professionally since 2012. He spent nine years working on the Coach magazine and website before moving to the fitness team at Tom’s Guide in 2024. Nick is a keen runner and also the founder of YouTube channel The Run Testers, which specialises in reviewing running shoes, watches, headphones and other gear.

Nick ran his first marathon in 2016 and became obsessed with the sport. He now has PBs of 2hr 25min for the marathon and 15min 30sec for 5K. Nick is also a qualified Run Leader in the UK.

Nick is an established expert in the fitness area and along with writing for many publications, including Live Science, Expert Reviews, Wareable, Coach and Get Sweat Go, he has been quoted on The Guardian and The Independent.

Is SNL New Tonight? (November 21, 2026) Musical Guest, Host, Start Time

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's almost time to close out 2026, so there are only a handful of fresh episodes of "Saturday Night Live" left this year.
  • Recent findings suggest that but that's in the past, and "SNL" is always looking ahead to the next show.
  • There is no fresh episode of "SNL" on November 21, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's almost time to close out 2026, so there are only a handful of fresh episodes of "Saturday Night Live" left this year. NBC's staple late night sketch comedy show is at the moment in the middle of Season 52, and they're coming off quite a celebrated episode after comedian John Mulaney returned to host for a seventh time. Mulaney has become one of the most reliable returning hosts, which is why he's also one of the best "SNL" hosts of all time.

Recent findings suggest that but that's in the past, and "SNL" is always looking ahead to the next show. As we head into the busy holiday season, you're probably wondering when you can take a break and catch some laughs with a latest episode of "SNL." Plus, you don't have time to wait and see whether there's a new episode when Saturday night rolls around. That's why we're here to let you know if there's a new "SNL" on November 21, 2026, as well as keep you posted on what's coming up next for "SNL.".

There is no fresh episode of "SNL" on November 21, 2026.

John Mulaney's episode was the last of three consecutive episodes running from Halloween through mid-November, and it's rare that executive producer Lorne Michaels pushes the cast and crew to do more than that in a row, as the series is truly exhausting to produce each week. (You can learn more about how the show is produced through a series of "SNL" documentaries available on Peacock that chronicle exactly how the show's team makes it happen over and over again.).

You would do well to check out John Mulaney's episode, if you haven't already, because it delivered the best episode of the season, including this sketch that every family is probably fighting about:.

Plus, let's not forget that Mulaney delivered what has now become a traditional New York-based musical sketch, including a special guest appearance by former cast member Bowen Yang:.

Since Thanksgiving is coming up, "SNL" is taking a short break before returning for several more episodes in December. Speaking of which...

In a recent development, "SNL" will be back with a fresh episode on December 5. More than likely, we'll get another three episodes in a row before Lorne Michaels gives the cast and crew their traditional holiday break over Christmas and through New Year into mid-to-late January. There's a chance we might only get two, since the third Saturday would be December 19, and that's pretty close to Christmas, but we don't know for sure yet.

When "SNL" returns on December 5, the episode will be hosted be someone who has been drumming up a lot of buzz, thanks to their appearance in a highly discussed movie that's still in theaters now.

In a recent development, amanda Seyfried will be making her hosting debut on the December 5 episode. Yes, this is the first time Seyfried has hosted the show. In fact, this is the first time she'll be making any appearance on "SNL," having never previously made a cameo in other episodes. But she's proven to be funny in comedies like "Mean Girls" and "Ted 2" (pictured above) over the years, so we're excited to see what she can do on "SNL.".

Seyfried is currently riding high after a (SPOILER ALERT) riveting appearance in "You Can See Everything," the documentary from directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder that follows convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares to serve her federal prison sentence. Seyfried's role in the movie is so compelling and unique that some are wondering if there's potential for her to get a Best Supporting Actress nomination (she partakes in pivotal reenactments that help define the movie's fascinating framework and revelations).

Sources indicate that in addition, Seyfried voices Cinderella in an animated Netflix movie called "Steps," hitting the streaming service starting on November 20, and she also stars in "The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd," a newly introduced movie written and directed by actor Tim Blake Nelson. The latter has been playing film festivals across the country, but it's not clear if it will be given an awards qualifying release in theaters otherwise before the end of 2026.

Seyfried will be joined by musical guest Don Toliver, a rapper whose fifth studio release, "Octane," became his first number one album this year.

"SNL" typically starts at 11:30pm ET, though that can potentially get disrupted by live sporting events or breaking news, which can delay the show slightly. However, in those cases, the show still unfolds live, but it's tape-delayed for those who will be watching "live" on NBC and/or Peacock.

When "SNL" is airing live, you can watch either on NBC through your usual television provider or by streaming live through Peacock.

Don't worry if you're not at home when the show starts at 11:30pm ET. NBC uploads upcoming sketches to YouTube not long after their air live. Plus, full new episodes are available to watch on Peacock the next day.

In addition, Peacock holds a library of old "SNL" episodes from across the show's decades-spanning history. However, those episodes don't always have all the sketches or musical performances due to complicated licensing rights for music.

For those who might like a little comedic flavor from across the pond, there's also "Saturday Night Live UK." Though you can't easily watch live here in the United States, new episodes of "SNL UK" hit Peacock on Sunday evenings the day after new episodes air.

After you watch the latest episode of "SNL," be sure to check out "The Ten to One Podcast," featuring me as one of the hosts recapping and reviewing new episodes of "SNL.".

Stay tuned for the latest details on when "SNL" has a new episode, right here at /Film.

I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the newly introduced static site generator they wrote to make it.
  • It has been revealed that earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online.
  • Industry observers note that when it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the newly introduced static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isnât exactly that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that itâs not about this websiteâ¦.

It has been revealed that earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I donât much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So Iâd been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, âWhere did you paint this?â Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that Iâd need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!

Industry observers note that when it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: âIsnât this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.â.

Recent findings suggest that the other is the Aesthetic Wolf: âThis should be a static website. The content almost never changes.â.

According to recent reports, yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the userâs browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is open followed by sendfile inside the event loop (Iâm joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.

But the problem with a static website is that for every latest post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for whatâs essentially a CRUD app is â¦ probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, thatâs not a static website any more.

Now look at this colorful house!

So what I really want is a website thatâs static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.

Hereâs my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. Iâm sure the design Iâm about to describe isnât novel, but I did come up with it. Iâm just pleased by it because itâs an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. Itâs dollar-efficient for me, i.e., itâs free*. Itâs resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And itâs fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.

It has been revealed that (Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is right now free, but if I paint enough then Iâll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.).

In a recent development, the main idea is that every html page is rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflareâs infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a new art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. Thatâs it.

According to recent reports, thereâs one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image at upload time, and I actually do it on the clientâs browser. Since Iâm the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflareâs R2, their S3-equivalent.

It has been revealed that why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service thatâll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and itâll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so itâs faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesnât add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.

All the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for pieces tagged #summer, a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflareâs CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing thatâs not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.

The website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the clientâs browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They donât write anything back to the server, so thereâs no database or anything. Theyâre just displaying the information in different ways. For example, hereâs an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I havenât uploaded everything Iâve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.

According to recent reports, (To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesnât read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.).

In a recent development, hereâs what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:.

Industry observers note that this is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Hereâs the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.

In my case, however, dependencies arenât explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but itâs so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.

So while itâs true that adding a fresh piece only changes the #evening page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasnât changed, so it doesnât need to be updated on every edge machine.

Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:.

And hereâs the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:.

In a recent development, by the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so theyâre pretty nicely integrated. But you donât really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.
